title: Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan: A Synthetic Dataset Capturing Japan's Demographics and Financial Context
abstract: Back to Articles Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan: A Synthetic Dataset Capturing Japan's Demographics and Financial Context Enterprise + Article Published November 9, 2026 Upvote 9 +3 Atsunori Fujita Atsunori Follow nvidia Masaya Ogushi SnowMasaya Follow nvidia Vincent Gong vg1024 Follow nvidia Kotaro Yamamoto kyamamoto-nv Follow nvidia Yoshi Suhara suhara Follow nvidia Will Jennings WillJenningsDC Follow nvidia Yev Meyer nv-3mei Follow nvidia A compound AI approach to Japanese personas grounded in real-world distributions Open Data Breaking Down Privacy Barriers to Pave the Way for AI in Finance In the financial sector, the utilization of real-world data faces significant constraints due to strict privacy regulations, compliance requirements, and the need for advanced domain expertise. In this context, the development of agentic AI in the financial domain requires synthetic data capable of avoiding the risks of using real data while reflecting demographics, household structures, and asset statuses to reproduce diverse, realistic financial scenarios. To address these challenges, Elith and NVIDIA have released Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan , a financial domain extension of the open-source persona dataset " Nemotron-Personas-Japan ." To our knowledge, it is the first open persona dataset at million-record scale that pairs Japan’s official statistics with household finance and financial literacy data. Built upon official government statistics, this dataset was developed using NeMo SDG-PGMs , a probabilistic graphical model framework for synthetic data generation (SDG), and NeMo Data Designer , an enterprise synthetic data generation system. Furthermore, to enhance the practical utility of the dataset in financial use cases, it was designed by incorporating insights and feedback provided by leading domestic financial institutions and industry associations, including Sompo Japan, Tokio Marine Holdings, Bank of Fukuoka, Mizuho Financial Group, Meiji Yasuda Life Insurance, and the Financial Data Utilization Association (FDUA). This dataset expands the environment where Japanese developers and enterprises can develop and evaluate AI tailored to local and industry requirements, without using real customer data. Released under the CC BY 4.0 license, it is available for commercial use. From building conversational agents to customer simulation and model evaluation, it supports practical financial AI development . The Nemotron-Personas collection , including Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan, is designed to seamlessly integrate with the user simulation framework NeMo User Sim , enabling instant execution of simulations drawn from diverse distributions consistent with the real world. What’s in the Dataset? 9M personas total (1M records x 9 personas each), written in natural Japanese 50 fields per record : 9 persona fields, 11 persona attributes, and 30 contextual fields based on official demographic and labor statistics ~1.5B tokens total , including ~750M persona tokens ~950k unique names 1600+ occupation categories reflecting Japan's workforce Comprehensive coverage across demographic, regional, asset distribution, and personality trait axes Diverse persona types : Occupations, sports, arts, travel, cooking, finance, financial behavior, and financial concerns Natural language persona attributes : Cultural background, skills and expertise, career goals and aspirations, hobbies and interests, household/parental/financial background, attitudes toward money, and financial planning Available for both commercial and non-commercial use under the CC BY 4.0 license How We Built It Data Generation Pipeline It was built using NVIDIA’s framework for synthetic data generation, NeMo Data Designer . This compound AI system enables complex Jinja templating, Pydantic validation, structured outputs, automated retries, and support for multiple generation backends. This is the essential toolset required for generating such large-scale synthetic datasets. In addition, the following models were utilized: NeMo SDG-PGMs (Apache-2.0) : A probabilistic graphical model framework for statistically grounded data generation gemma-4-31B-it (Apache-2.0) : For Japanese text generation Enhanced Cultural Context Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan was designed to align with Japan's official demographic and labor statistics while taking into account key considerations essential for AI training: Education : Where national statistics broadly aggregate degree levels, we introduced finer granularity to enable the model to reflect diverse educational pathways. Occupation : We incorporated additional categories (such as business owners and specialized professions) to broaden the spectrum of occupations used for training. Life Stages : We modeled scenarios that rarely surface prominently in statistics, such as students, retirees, and periods of unemployment, to represent more realistic personas. Household Finances : In addition to individual income and spending propensity, we incorporated household-level financial and real assets to replicate diverse economic backgrounds. Digital & Financial Literacy : By including internet and smartphone usage along with financial literacy, we enabled the model to precisely capture consumer profiles in financial use cases. Private By Design Every persona is fully synthetic. No real individuals are represented, and the dataset is designed to reduce privacy risk. Demographics and household finances follow official statistics and public survey data, and names follow real Japanese naming patterns. Personas are built from these distributions, not from records about real people. Who This Data Is For Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan is built first for teams creating financial AI in Japan, at banks and insurers and at the startups and integrators that serve them. Each persona carries household finances and financial literacy alongside demographics. Teams can use them to build customer-service agents, evaluate sales conversations/marketing initiatives, run user simulations in NeMo User Sim, and red-team customer-facing AI. The release also serves anyone building for Japanese users. It holds 9M personas, 50% more than Nemotron-Personas-Japan, across 50 fields instead of 22. That gives any Japanese-language project finer slices of the population to train and test on. Practical AI Applications The synthetic personas in this dataset can be leveraged for: Multi-turn conversation : Using personas as "seeds" to generate human-like dialogue datasets. Domain-specific AI development : Generating datasets to build AI assistants tailored to realistic scenarios in financial use cases. Bias testing and fairness : Evaluating how models and AI agent systems perform across rural and urban divides, various age groups, educational backgrounds, and economic circumstances to check whether AI performs consistently across Japanese society. Why It Matters Access to diverse, high-quality training data that reflects real-world populations has long been a challenge in AI development. Enterprise AI development has predominantly relied on private data, creating barriers for researchers, startups, and particularly AI developers in regions with limited available data. Data Diversity : Reflects the full spectrum of Japan's population, which helps reduce biased training and the risk of model collapse . Cultural Authenticity : Reduces reliance on Western-centric datasets and supports the development of Sovereign AI systems . Privacy and Governance : Aligned with Japan’s innovation-first approach to AI governance. Every persona is synthetic, so no customer data is needed to build or test with it. By releasing Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan under CC BY 4.0, we provide access to enterprise-grade, high-quality synthetic data, empowering anyone to build culturally grounded AI systems with lower cost and less privacy risk. Pairs with Nemotron-PII-Japan Nemotron-PII-Japan launches the same day.

title: Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together
abstract: Back to Articles Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together Enterprise Article Published November 9, 2026 Upvote 4 Alex M Tseng alexmtseng Follow amazon Higher-Order Pruning of Experts in Mixture-of-Experts Language Models Introduction Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token. For example, Qwen3.5-122B has 256 experts in each of its 48 MoE layers, and 95% of its ~250 GB parameter memory footprint is taken up entirely by these expert MLPs alone. However, for any given token, only 8 experts in each layer are actually used. Expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck. That is, permanently delete the least useful experts. Pruning avoids the latency issues which make dynamic loading/off-loading of experts impractical; it does not require any training; and it composes with quantization . Given these attractive benefits and the simplicity of the idea, it's easy to see why expert pruning has become a go-to approach for shrinking MoEs. The difficulty lies in deciding which experts are safest to remove. Existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least important experts (in each layer independently). These are first-order methods, because they assume each expert's contribution is independent of all others. In reality, experts form cooperative groups. We observe consistent clusters of co-activated experts in our own experiments, and independent work has shown that expert cooperation is a stable property of MoEs and is important for model performance . Ignoring these interactions leads to suboptimal pruning, especially at aggressive rates. Our newest paper derives HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts), a second-order method that accounts for pairwise expert interactions. At 50% pruning, HOPE achieves the best average rank of any method, with gains of up to +6.1% on agentic coding tasks over the next-best pruning method. In this post, we explain how HOPE works, show where it outperforms existing methods, and walk through how to use it for your own models. For readers unfamiliar with MoE architectures, see Mixture of Experts (MoEs) in Transformers . Experts don't work alone In a standard MoE, each layer has E E E experts, and each input token x x x is routed independently to K K K such experts ( K = 8 K = 8 K = 8 is a typical choice). Routing is performed by a single layer which produces softmax-normalized gate weights g k ( x ) g_{k}(x) g k ​ ( x ) for each expert k k k , wherein the K K K experts with the highest gate weights are selected to form the active set of experts, T ( x ) ⊂ { 1 , . . , E } T(x) \subset\{1,..,E\} T ( x ) ⊂ { 1 , .. , E } . The output of the layer is then ∑ k ∈ T ( x ) g k ( x ) f k ( x ) \sum\limits_{k\in T(x)}g_{k}(x)f_{k}(x) k ∈ T ( x ) ∑ ​ g k ​ ( x ) f k ​ ( x ) , where f k ( x ) f_{k}(x) f k ​ ( x ) is the output of expert k k k for token x x x . Left: typical MoE layer, where each token is routed to the top-K experts. Right: first-order methods rank and delete experts based on a scalar importance score, but the best pruning decisions will also consider the strength of interactions between experts. Importantly, experts in the selected set T ( x ) T(x) T ( x ) are not independent. Experts form stable cooperative groups that get consistently co-activated together. This has been observed before in the literature , as well: expert co-selection patterns emerge early in training and stabilize throughout. This means that when we prune experts from an MoE layer, pruning decisions need to consider the higher-order effects between these experts. Removing expert A might seem fine on its own, but if expert B—which frequently cooperates with and relies on A—is highly important, then removing A would dismantle a cooperative group just through a single deletion. First-order methods miss this entirely, because they score A and B separately. This effect compounds at high pruning rates. When we remove up to 50% of experts, we risk breaking many cooperative links. This is where second-order pruning is most advantageous. How HOPE identifies a prune-set (See Appendix A in our corresponding paper for the full derivation of the HOPE objective) When we delete a set of P P P experts from some MoE layer, the selected set of experts T ( x ) T(x) T ( x ) (for any token x x x ) can change. The pruned experts that would have been selected are replaced by the experts with the next-highest gate weights. The resulting change in layer output is the pruning error . Our goal is to find the prune-set P P P (of some predefined pruning budget ∣ P ∣ \vert P\vert ∣ P ∣ ) that minimizes the resulting pruning error (over tokens x x x from our calibration set). Unfortunately, minimizing the pruning error over P P P directly is intractable. The pruning error depends on the identities of the replacement experts, which in turn depend on the prune-set P P P itself. HOPE sidesteps this by defining a tractable surrogate Z Z Z , which strictly upper-bounds the dominant component of the pruning error: Z = [ ∑ j ∈ P ∩ T ( x ) g j ( x ) ∥ f j ( x ) ∥ 2 ] 2 ≥ true error Z = \bigl[\sum\limits_{j \in P\cap T(x)} g_{j}(x)\Vert f_j(x)\Vert_{2}\bigr]^{2} \geq \text{true error} Z = [ j ∈ P ∩ T ( x ) ∑ ​ g j ​ ( x ) ∥ f j ​ ( x ) ∥ 2 ​ ] 2 ≥ true error Because Z Z Z is a squared sum, expanding it naturally produces cross-terms g i ( x ) g j ( x ) ∥ f i ( x ) ∥ 2 ∥ f j ( x ) ∥ 2 g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2} g i ​ ( x ) g j ​ ( x ) ∥ f i ​ ( x ) ∥ 2 ​ ∥ f j ​ ( x ) ∥ 2 ​ between pairs of experts. These are the interaction terms that first-order methods discard. To find the optimal prune-set, HOPE minimizes E [ Z ] \mathbb{E}[Z] E [ Z ] over the calibration set, which can be reformulated as the following quadratic program: P ∗ = arg min ⁡ p p ⊤ F p s.t. p ∈ { 0 , 1 } E , ∑ k = 1 E p k = ∣ P ∣ P^{*} = \argmin_{p}\; p^{\top}Fp \quad \text{s.t.} \quad p \in \{0,1\}^{E}, \sum\limits_{k=1}^{E}p_{k} = \vert P\vert P ∗ = p arg min ​ p ⊤ F p s.t. p ∈ { 0 , 1 } E , k = 1 ∑ E ​ p k ​ = ∣ P ∣ where F ∈ R E × E F\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times E} F ∈ R E × E is defined as: F i , j = 1 ∣ X i , j ∣ ∑ x ∈ X i , j g i ( x ) g j ( x ) ∥ f i ( x ) ∥ 2 ∥ f j ( x ) ∥ 2 where X i , j = { x : i , j ∈ T ( x ) } F_{i,j} = \frac{1}{\vert \mathcal{X}_{i,j}\vert} \sum\limits_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{i,j}} g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}\quad\text{where}\quad \mathcal{X}_{i,j} = \{x: i,j \in T(x)\} F i , j ​ = ∣ X i , j ​ ∣ 1 ​ x ∈ X i , j ​ ∑ ​ g i ​ ( x ) g j ​ ( x ) ∥ f i ​ ( x ) ∥ 2 ​ ∥ f j ​ ( x ) ∥ 2 ​ where X i , j ​ = { x : i , j ∈ T ( x )} This F-matrix is collected on the calibration dataset, and the optimal prune-set is obtained by solving the resulting quadratic program (QP) with a continuous relaxation (then rounding to binary solutions). Each entry F i , j F_{i,j} F i , j ​ captures the average gate-weighted output product of experts i i i and j j j , across tokens where both are co-activated. title: Google Unveils TPU 8i Max and TPU 8tx: A Dual-Chip TPU and a Confidential TPU
abstract: Google has added two new systems to its eighth-generation TPU lineup. TPU 8i Max targets massive context windows and rack density. TPU 8tx targets secure, confidential inference. Google TPU 8i Max is a dual-chip package built from 2 TPU 8i chips. Both arrive alongside TPU 8t and TPU 8i, announced in April . Google announced both systems today. These are new system configurations, not new chips. Google reuses its existing eighth-generation silicon and changes packaging, hosts, memory and networking around it. TPU 8i Max attacks the memory wall. Google team combines 2 low-latency TPU 8i chips onto 1 package. The result doubles compute, SRAM and HBM bandwidth compared with TPU 8i. Each TPU 8i chip is rated at 10.1 PFLOPS of FP4, 288 GB of HBM and 8,601 GB/s . It also carries 384 MB of on-chip SRAM. Doubling those figures implies about 20.2 PFLOPS FP4, 768 MB SRAM and 17.2 TB/s per package. Google did not publish these absolute figures. It also did not state HBM capacity for TPU 8i Max. TPU 8i Max fits twice the silicon in the existing rack footprint. Google positions it for agents working across whole codebases or hours of video. TPU 8tx is built for regulated enterprises and governments. It keeps data and model weights protected even while in active use. Normally, data must be decrypted in memory during processing. TPU 8tx uses the same silicon as TPU 8t . It pairs that silicon with 5th Gen AMD EPYC CPU hosts. It also adopts the Boardfly network from TPU 8i. Google claims up to 2x lower latency than TPU 8t, with a near-zero security penalty. Teams can fine-tune, distill and run reinforcement learning on 1 system. That avoids moving sensitive data between separate clusters. On Qwen3 235B, TPU Sync dropped median KV transfer latency from several seconds to about 230 ms. TTFT fell 60% on average for 235B and 90% for 480B under low concurrency. These tests ran on Ironwood (TPU v7x), not the new systems. Derived = 2x Google’s published TPU 8i per-chip figures. TPU 8t values come from Google’s technical deep dive . Check out the official announcement , the TPU 8t and 8i deep dive , and the TPU Sync repo . title: Baidu’s ERNIE Evolve Automated Research System Beats NanoChat and NanoGPT Records
abstract: Baidu has just released ERNIE Evolve , an automated research system that improves AI training and inference code. Given a repository, an objective and evaluation criteria, it picks research directions, edits code and runs experiments. Only changes that pass a hidden evaluator and a separate reviewer are kept. Baidu team tested the ERNIE Evolve automated research system on three public benchmarks. It then optimized inference for ERNIE-5.5-Flash, still in development. ERNIE Evolve is an automated research system from Baidu that optimizes code against a fixed, measurable objective. Baidu announced it on X as a practical step toward recursive self-improvement (RSI). In RSI, AI systems improve the software that builds and serves AI. The system runs 2 nested loops. The outer loop decides what to investigate. The inner loop develops and tests improvements inside each direction. Several research lanes run in parallel, each with its own tree of code versions. Failed experiments are recorded, so later rounds can avoid repeating them. Baidu ran the same loop on NanoChat AutoResearch , NanoGPT Speedrun and SOL-ExecBench . Recursive and Hyra-1.0 Speedrun times were set against the older ~79.7 s record, so they are not like-for-like. Hyra SOL self-report via Tencent coverage . Baidu team then pointed the system at 3 live engineering tasks on ERNIE-5.5-Flash. Baselines had already been tuned by engineers. title: Reason Machines Open-Sources Aspen, a Git Server Built for AI Agents
abstract: Reason Machines has released Aspen , an open-source Git server for AI agent traffic. It targets repositories that hundreds of agents push to at once. Aspen independently implements the design OpenAI described for Pando. Aspen is a self-hostable Git server from Reason Machines that scales writes per branch, not per repository. It speaks plain Git over HTTPS and SSH. Packs go to S3-compatible object storage; branch history goes to PostgreSQL. An agent pushes every few minutes, and CI fetches after each push. Per Reason Machines , a classic server queues every push to a repository together. It also builds a fresh pack for every fetch. Server work grows with clients, not with new code. OpenAI hit this wall and built Pando. It cut median push latency by nearly 5x and serves nearly a petabyte daily. Aspen follows Pando and drops 2 claims most Git servers keep. Each branch is a chain of versions in one Postgres row. A push uploads its pack, then moves the branch with one compare-and-swap. Pushes to different branches never wait for each other. If 2 pushes race on one branch, one wins. The other gets Git’s usual “fetch first” error. The cost: branches may be read at slightly different moments. Aspen never unpacks a push. It checks the pack, completes missing bases and stores it as-is. A fetch streams stored packs the client lacks, recompressing nothing. Signed URLs can serve packs from a CDN. A push sees only the trunk branch, so negotiation stays small with a million branches. Background compaction merges packs 16 at a time, in levels like a log-structured merge tree. A client far behind gets a few dozen packs, not thousands. Depth-1 CI fetches get a tip pack built once and served to every job. The test used one 8-core server, S3 Standard and a 4-core Postgres. The target was a copy of git.git, about 4,500 files and 75,000 commits. Aspen sustained 567 pushes per second for 5 minutes with no errors. Each push reached S3 and Postgres before Git printed “ok.” Cursor reports up to 120 pushes per second for Origin on S3 Standard. On S3 Express One Zone it exceeds 300. That is a replicated cluster on Cursor’s monorepo, so setups differ. The README calls Aspen’s figures indicative, not performance claims. You build from source with Rust. aspen dev runs everything with SQLite and a local directory. Teams get Docker Compose with PostgreSQL and MinIO, plus a Helm chart. Terraform covers AWS, Google Cloud, Azure and Hetzner. Mirror mode fronts GitHub or GitLab, so you can trial it without migrating. The live demo is a 64 x 64 pixel canvas where each click is one pushed commit. Per the company, one Reason agent built Aspen from first commit to public in 4 days. That took 151 merged PRs. title: 0sec Labs Open-Sources 0, an AI Security Harness With Web UI, CLI and MCP
abstract: Zurich-based 0sec Labs has released 0 , an open-source AI security harness. It runs vulnerability investigations, code review, pentesting, reverse engineering and fix generation. Developers drive it from a local browser console, a headless CLI or an MCP server . The 0sec Labs open-source AI security harness is licensed MIT OR Apache-2.0 and ships as a research preview. 0 is a control plane around LLMs and security tools. It is not a model. You plug in a provider, and 0 runs scoped workflows against authorized targets. The research team describes it as a self-evolving, multi-model harness . 0sec Labs is backed by Y Combinator . The architecture docs state one rule: reproduce before trusting. Agentic scans follow a conceptual pipeline: Web pentesting is shell-first. The agent uses bash with curl, python3 and sqlmap, not a fixed HTTP tool set. Evidence carries a proof grade from candidate to impact-proven . Compiled targets go through 0verse , a separate in-repo engine. It wraps Ghidra, angr and AFL++. Its local MCP server exposes 9 tools for scanning, triage, PoVs and reports. Installation is one script. Running 0 opens the local browser console without an account. The console has chat, a findings queue and board, workflow templates, skills and memory. Coding agents connect through 0 mcp-server --workflows . The CLI exposes the same workflow runner with commands like 0 workflow run and 0 runs list . Model access is bring-your-own. The API keys page lists OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek, OpenRouter, Azure, Qwen, Kimi, GLM and Grok. It also supports Claude, Codex and Gemini CLI runtimes. All scores below are self-reported. The recorded cost was about $5.20 per solved XBOW challenge . The research page lists 30+ merged Linux kernel 0-days. Disclosures span Bluetooth, NFC, mac802154, TIPC and mlx5e subsystems. Library CVEs include jsonata, node-forge, protobuf.js and Wireshark. The open-source harness is free. You pay your model provider. A hosted version, 0cloud , is on a waitlist. The pricing page lists $100 in trial credits and $5 per PR security test. Check out the GitHub repo , docs and research disclosures . title: Testing Claude on real-world electronics design
abstract: 01 Reasoning through geometric problems A little over a year ago, we began testing how well Claude could design basic electronic circuits. We collaborated with Diode Computers , 1 a company that designs and manufactures circuit boards, to train Claude on simple tasks—for example, on reading a chip’s datasheet and working out which parts a chip needs in order to run. The models we experimented with back then couldn’t reliably lay out a circuit board; they also struggled to design components that fit together. Now, Claude can both design and prototype electronic hardware from start to finish. Engineering an electronic device requires working through many complex steps and practical constraints. You have to not only design and simulate a circuit board, but also reason about the board’s physical layout and how it will behave, model the mechanical components, and write firmware—all while keeping track of which parts are readily available and what a factory is set up to build. To see how newer Claude models have improved in this area, we collaborated with Diode again, this time asking Claude Fable 5.2 to design three electronic devices: a speakerphone, a voice-assistant hub, and a handheld virtual pet. With minimal prompting, Claude was able to use geometric reasoning to lay out each circuit board, anticipate manufacturing constraints, and make sure its designs would work within them. It revised its own work, modeled its designs in computer-aided design (CAD) software, and, finally, directed human engineers to build prototypes that worked without any fixes to their circuitry. For each design, we began by giving Claude a simple prompt that outlined what kind of device to build and its main hardware requirements. The prompt for the speakerphone, for example, asked for “a puck that plugs into a computer over USB-C and includes microphones and a speaker, supporting Bluetooth with a PCB antenna.” Claude proceeded to write the device’s specifications, draw clean visual schematics, choose where to place the components on a printed circuit board (PCB), route the copper connections between them, design a 3D-printable enclosure, code the firmware, and prepare a parts list. Diode assembled the circuit boards and ran the firmware, under Claude’s direction. The final result was a prototype of a speakerphone that still works after weeks of use. Claude went through a similar process to build the voice-assistant hub and the virtual pet, and both are also still in good working order. Because the devices are early prototypes, we don’t yet know how they’ll hold up with continued use or whether they would pass commercial certifications. The three devices built from Claude’s designs, from left to right: a battery-powered handheld pet, a home voice-assistant hub, and a USB speakerphone. Claude engineered the electronics and the enclosures and wrote firmware for each one. Reasoning through geometric problems The most substantial difference between Fable 5.2 and the models we used in our earlier tests was in how well Fable 5.2 reasoned through complex geometric problems, such as where to place components on a circuit board and how to route the copper connections between them. Earlier models had struggled to decide how to arrange basic components—placing supporting parts too far from the chips they served, for example, or orienting connectors incorrectly. Fable 5.2, by contrast, produced more compact, practical layouts. It routed the most important connections first: those that carry high-speed signals or high currents, or that are sensitive to noise. For example, for the voice-assistant hub, Claude started by routing the USB and Ethernet connections, which transmit signals along pairs of tracks—thin strips of copper on the board. It routed one pair of tracks at a time, keeping the two tracks in each pair the same length and correctly spaced. It also added tuning patterns—small zigzags that lengthen a track so that signals arrive at the same time—and arranged the parts of the power supply to make it more efficient. To demonstrate how much better Fable 5.2 is than earlier models at laying out circuit boards, we asked Diode to run PCB Gym—an internal benchmark that scores models based on how well they can place components and reroute connections on board designs whose layouts have been removed. Fable 5.2 scored 69% on the benchmark, compared with 25% for Fable 5 (Figure 2). It also performed better on BenchCAD 2.1 , a public benchmark that tests whether models can rebuild 3D parts, assemblies, and circuit boards from engineering drawings and rendered images. Fable 5.2 scored 83.5%, nearly double the score of its predecessor, Claude Fable 5.1. Scores plotted against total API cost for recent frontier models on Diode PCB Gym, a benchmark that instructs models to place components and route connections on circuit boards whose layouts have been removed. Revising designs Earlier models rarely revised their own work when designing PCB layouts, even when it became clear that their placement choices would never let them finish routing the connections. Over the past year, Diode designed many boards with these models that were 95% complete but still unusable. When Claude noticed one of its designs wasn’t working, it would change course without being prompted to do so. For instance, when designing the speakerphone’s circuit board, which has four layers of copper, it reassigned signals to different pins on two of the chips. This allowed the tracks under the speakerphone’s touch-sensitive controls to stay on a single layer without crossing one another. Later, when the back of the board became too crowded, Claude swapped the signals on interchangeable pins and laid out a whole corner of the board again, rather than patching the problem with extra jumps between layers. And when placing tracks in its design file for the voice-assistant hub, Claude noticed that the copper connections were “getting too tangled to trace visually” and reasoned, “I should just rip these traces [tracks] and start fresh.” It proceeded to delete and reroute copper connections dozens of times until it found an arrangement that worked. The routing for the voice-assistant hub before and after Claude reorganized the connections. Left: the microphone’s power track (blue lines) loops around the ground ring at the sound port, a front-side track (red) crosses the ring, and a via—a small hole that connects layers of copper—is placed between the microphone’s pads. Right: the same area after Claude rerouted the power track, with the ring clear and grounded. Claude’s reasoning for redoing the version on the left: “That’s risky placement under a bottom-port MEMS mic, even if clearance is technically fine, so I want to redo the local routing cleanly for both identical mic footprints.” Using software and documentation When a design decision for one of the devices depended on the details of a particular part, Claude often checked that part’s datasheet—a technical document published by the manufacturer. When asked whether the handheld pet would work without a battery, Claude read the charger’s datasheet and answered that it would run on USB power but predicted that the charging light would flicker, because the charger keeps recharging a small capacitor in the battery’s place. 2 To route the connections on the voice-assistant hub, Claude started with the design software Diode provided, which let it run the router (a tool for drawing tracks) built into KiCad, a widely used circuit board design program. KiCad’s router drew one track at a time between two points Claude chose. But the hub had long tracks running from a 100-pin connector, and Claude judged that routing these one by one would take too much step-by-step guidance. Instead, Claude wrote its own router: an algorithm that divides the board into a grid and searches it to find a clear path for each track.

title: Introducing Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2
abstract: We’ve upgraded Claude Fable and Claude Mythos—models that are designed to tackle the most daunting technical challenges. Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision. During prerelease testing they’ve helped our engineers complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours—among many other applications we’ll discuss below. Claude Fable and Claude Mythos are the same underlying model. Fable has strong cybersecurity and biology safeguards to guard against misuse, which allows us to make it available to all users. Organizations pursuing beneficial applications in cybersecurity or biomedical research can apply for access to Mythos through our recently expanded Life Sciences and Cyber Verification Programs. Testers have found that Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 communicate more clearly than past Fable and Mythos models. They generate outputs up to 30% faster than Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1, and they’re available at a lower price: $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 also come with an optional fast mode, which speeds up token generation by up to 2.5 times. Fast mode is available for $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens. Safety and alignment. To help ensure safety and alignment keep step with growing model capabilities, we ran extensive prerelease safety testing on the model that underlies Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. This included developing novel evaluations that give deeper insight into specific concerning behaviors like sandbox escapes. We believe high-stakes risks from misalignment remain low, and the model performed as well as, or better than, our recent models on most alignment measures. Fable 5.2’s cyber and biology safeguards are as robust as those of Fable 5.1 but produce fewer unnecessary blocks, and we have implemented our strongest-ever protections against distillation attacks. We describe more about our safety testing below, and full details can be found in the Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 System Card . When to use Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. Fable and Mythos are best for the most ambitious, open-ended technical work. For most coding and knowledge tasks, we recommend that users start with Claude Opus 5.5, our strongest daily driver, and then switch to a different model as required, depending on the scope and complexity of their work—upward to Fable or Mythos, or downward to Claude Sonnet 5.5 or Claude Haiku 5.5. Fable 5.2 can also play the role of Advisor (where Haiku, Sonnet, or Opus models consult it to help solve harder problems) or Orchestrator (where it delegates simpler tasks to smaller models).
