title: JPMorganChase expands Claude Code to more employees across the firm
abstract: JPMorganChase is rolling out Claude across the firm, to more employees beyond engineers. In the Commercial and Investment Bank, work moves into production faster, and the firm redeploys that capacity against its business priorities. Teams are modernizing other legacy systems, and engineers are building their own agents, including pull request review and self-healing agents, and sharing what works. Infrastructure and operations teams use Claude Code (opens in new tab) for monitoring, alerting and root cause analysis. The firm's security team uses our frontier models to find and fix vulnerabilities faster, work we first described in Project Glasswing (opens in new tab) . Reaching product teams and advisors The people closest to the business are building with Claude too. Product teams turn requirements directly into engineering backlogs, and other teams use Claude Code for risk and controls assessments and program planning. Knowledge work is already underway. Much of the product development lifecycle happens outside the code: research, requirements, design and planning. In their Asset & Wealth Management business, JPMorganChase is putting the people with the deepest business insight and the boldest ideas alongside their technology and product experts into small, empowered teams. This is helping them to more easily build and deliver customized client investment solutions at scale. Claude Code is now part of their engineering workflow, and teams are moving faster while putting every change through more rigorous testing before it reaches clients. Last month, J.P. Morgan Asset Management announced a connector that brings 55ip's ActiveTax Technology® into Claude for Financial Advisors (opens in new tab) , putting tax-aware portfolio transition analysis into advisors' daily work. Built for a regulated firm Claude Code runs in controlled environments, including Devspace, the firm’s containerized development platform, on its own infrastructure. The intent is to prevent agents from getting direct access to employee credentials or internal systems. Access widens in stages, and new Claude models go through the firm’s own approval process before anyone there can use them. Code ships under the same discipline. Thousands of automated tests and approval gates check every change, and an automated gate returns a hard pass or halt that the pipeline enforces, so Claude can't sign off on its own work. People stay accountable for every production change. Over the past year, JPMorganChase’s use of Claude has grown from software engineering to cyber defense to tools for financial advisors, and what JPMorganChase asks of us is shaping what we build for other regulated institutions. Claude working inside the controls of one of the world’s largest financial institutions is what we are building toward.

title: Make a Robot Arm Feel Weightless with NVIDIA Holoscan 5
abstract:
Picture guiding a robot arm by hand while its motors supply just enough torque to support its weight and keep the robot upright. This simple interaction, a useful starting point for robots that learn by demonstration, manipulate objects, or work alongside people, depends on a gravity-compensation loop. Building such a loop is only possible by continuously calculating the inverse dynamics of the system based on precise models of all the links of the robot arm, their dimensions, masses, and moments of inertia. This calculation, which needs to be done rapidly with low jitter, requires knowing the current state of the robot, so gravity-comp demos are an excellent proof of life for both the robot model and the runtime that’s executing these algorithms. NVIDIA Holoscan 5 introduced robotic control alongside streamlined sensor processing. In this tutorial, we’ll build custom Holoscan SDK operators and wire them into a graph. We’ll test the code on a real robot and use the Holoscan SDK’s built-in Nsight Systems annotations to inspect latency and jitter. This walkthrough has been tested on Jetson Orin Nano, Jetson Thor, and x86 Ubuntu 24.04 systems. Why Holoscan? Video 1. A responsive robot with Holoscan installed for gravity compensation workload vs. a custom script runtime Holoscan SDK brings low-latency control and high-throughput perception into one programming model , with execution paths designed for CPU- and GPU-based workloads. Its goal is a transparent runtime: minimize avoidable framework overhead while making application execution explicit and inspectable. Keep the control path focused on the work. Holoscan uses partitions to group chains of operators on a single thread, avoiding cross-thread handoffs and unnecessary syscalls, reducing latency and jitter. Clock and data-arrival triggers express when work should run, while bounded, drop-oldest queues prevent outdated work from accumulating. Bring existing algorithms and code rather than rewriting them for a framework. Holoscan 5 has a new, lightweight programming model that can be easily integrated into existing code bases, and it’s never been easier to get data into and out of Holoscan graphs. Add perception without adopting a different programming model. Whether you’re handling 10 kHz CPU-centric motor control loops, heavy-throughput GPU algorithms, or AI inference, Holoscan lets developers and their agents clearly express execution intent using the same operators, ports, and graph APIs, logically splitting their workloads into separate graphs that can coexist, with the ability to pin partitions to dedicated CPU cores, CUDA green contexts, or even execute as a CUDA graph. Inspect the plan, then measure the result. Operators express their intent with timing contracts, and before the first run, the compiled plan exposes how the application will execute and catches configuration errors before deployment. This means agents and developers can quickly iterate on a design without ever deploying to real hardware. Plus, built-in NVTX annotations make operator execution and message transfers visible in Nsight Systems. Developers can examine host control-path latency and update jitter, then repeat those measurements as the application grows. An accessible platform for torque-control development This tutorial is built around the Seeed Studio reBot Arm B601-DM , which is an accessible, affordable platform for getting started with modern robotics control. Most low-cost robot arm development platforms use highly-geared hobby servos, which are only suitable for positional control. The reBot Arm uses quasi-direct-drive (QDD) actuators that provide high torque bandwidth for both control and sensing — important for haptic, co-bot, or other torque-oriented projects like this one. Starting off with gravity-comp Before adding perception pipelines, motion planners, and other higher-level controls, building a basic gravity compensation loop helps provide a useful (and entertaining!) sanity-check for whether your simulation model accurately describes the physical robot. While position-control examples can mask problems with joint axes, offsets, link placements, masses, and moments, all of these affect the required torque in instantly-observable ways; any bugs in DH parameters or mass properties can make the arm sag or push upward as its pose changes. Even if your end application doesn’t need gravity-comp, torque control lets us shape how the robot responds to forces—a key ingredient in safer interaction between humans and co-bots. Our arm combines gravity feedforward with light stiffness and damping, so it supports its weight while yielding to a person’s hand. That flexibility makes timing critical. Tracking a position through torque commands requires rapid, consistent feedback at hundreds or thousands of Hz, and runtime overhead and thread handoffs can add phase lag and jitter that cause the robot to become unstable. This tutorial uses Pinocchio as the inverse-dynamics solver. It loads the robot’s URDF model and provides a Recursive Newton–Euler Algorithm (RNEA) solver, which calculates joint torques for specified positions, velocities, and accelerations. We also use the motorbridge library to read joint feedback and send commands to the arm’s motors. Set up the Python example This walkthrough uses Holoscan’s Python API. The tutorial repository also contains a complete C++ implementation , with its own build instructions . Both implement the same three-operator control loop. Use Python 3.12 or newer on Linux. From the repository root: python3.12 -m venv build/python-venv
build/python-venv/bin/python -m pip install --only-binary=:all: -r requirements-python.txt
build/python-venv/bin/python -m pip check Check the serial device and motor IDs in the arm’s configuration file. The tutorial repository’s technical guide covers configuration, the math, and hardware startup. Express the control loop as three operators Holoscan 5 has two programming concepts: Operators and Graphs. To read the robot’s state, calculate the command using the inverse-dynamics solver, and send it to the arm, we can decompose that problem into three operators wired into a graph: Figure 1. Closed loop control system diagram Operators are subclassed from Operator and have three important methods to implement: Method Purpose setup() Declare input and output ports. contract() Declare when to run and which input data to use. compute() Read input(s), do work, and publish output(s). Table 1. Core methods to implement for custom Holoscan operators Here are outlines of the three operators to build: 1. Read joint state on a clock JointStateSourceOp declares one output in setup() . Its OnClock contract requests a tick every 2.5 ms (we’re running this demo at 400 Hz). Each compute() reads all seven motors and emits their state: import holoscan as hsdk class JointStateSourceOp(hsdk.Operator): state = hsdk.Output("state", hsdk.pyobject) def setup(self, spec): spec.output(self.state) def contract(self): return hsdk.Contract().trigger(hsdk.OnClock(period=hsdk.time.us(2500))) def start(self): self.sequence = 0 def compute(self, ctx): self.sequence += 1 self.state.emit(robot.read_state(self.sequence)) 2. Compute gravity compensation when state arrives PinocchioGravityOp declares a state input and command output. OnEach runs it when state arrives. The hsdk.Param declarations expose gains, torque scaling, and joint direction as operator parameters: class PinocchioGravityOp(hsdk.Operator): state = hsdk.Input("state", hsdk.pyobject) command = hsdk.Output("command", hsdk.pyobject) kp = hsdk.Param(1.5, range=(0.0, 500.0)) kd = hsdk.Param(1.0, range=(0.0, 5.0)) tau_scale = hsdk.Param([1.0] * 6) joint_direction = hsdk.Param([1.0] * 6) def setup(self, spec): spec.input(self.state, queue_depth=1) spec.output(self.command) def contract(self): return hsdk.Contract().trigger(hsdk.OnEach(self.state)) def compute(self, ctx): state = self.state.receive_data() command = controller.

title: How skills and agents work in AWS Quick
abstract: If you use AI agents, you’ve probably explained the same task more than once. You might describe how to build your weekly status update, write release notes, manage a project, or create tickets. These are all repeatable tasks that you can encode using AWS Quick through agents and skills. AWS Quick is an AI-powered service for automating tasks, analyzing data, building web applications, and conducting research. You work with it in natural language, and Quick uses AI agents to process your requests against your connected data sources and applications. In this post, we cover how agents, skills, and your data fit together in AWS Quick, and how to build and share skills that work for your team. We also show how the official catalog and custom agents help you put those skills to use. In this section, we explain the foundational concepts that help you understand AWS Quick in relation to agents, skills, and your data. Figure 1: How a Quick agent follows its instructions, loads the skills a task needs, acts through connectors, and grounds its answers in your data The agent sits at the center of Figure 1. It follows its instructions, loads the skills that a task calls for, takes action through connectors, and grounds its answers in your data: spaces, knowledge bases, datasets, and dashboards. An agent in AWS Quick is a configurable AI with its own instructions, knowledge sources (spaces), and connectors, which it uses to answer questions and get work done for you. You can work with an agent in chat, or let it run on its own using a routine . Agents can only reach the resources and services that you can, and you decide what each agent is allowed to do. Quick is the default built-in agent that every user has access to. It has no fixed scope, so in each conversation it works with whatever resources you have access to, such as your spaces, knowledge bases, dashboards, connectors, and skills. You don’t need to decide in advance which data or tools a request needs, so you can start most work with Quick. A custom agent is one that you or someone on your team configures for a specific job. An example is a human resources (HR) onboarding assistant that answers new-hire questions from the HR team’s space. You give it its own instructions and limit it to the spaces, connectors, and skills that your use case requires. After you test and publish it, you can share it with other users and groups within your AWS Quick account. For a walkthrough of building one, see Build AI-powered employee onboarding agents with AWS Quick . Agents ground their answers in the data you connect to Quick. A space is a curated collection of documents and AWS Quick resources that an agent uses as a source of information. You can create one for yourself, your team, or another group in your organization. You can upload files and folders to a space, or add assets such as dashboards, knowledge bases, action connectors, and datasets. When you start a conversation with Quick, you can attach a space to narrow the data that Quick uses for that conversation. When you add a space to an agent, the space becomes part of the agent’s configuration, and the agent draws on it when a request needs it. A knowledge base is an organized, indexed collection of documents or content from data sources, optimized for retrieval and question answering. Quick syncs knowledge bases from sources such as Google Drive, Microsoft OneDrive, Confluence, Microsoft SharePoint, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), web crawler, or Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases . Quick keeps them up to date on a sync schedule. Datasets and dashboards come from AWS Quick Sight , the business intelligence feature in Quick, which is available in accounts provisioned through the AWS Management Console. A dataset is a prepared collection of data ready for use in analyses and dashboards. A dashboard is the published version of an analysis that you share with other Quick users. With datasets, you can build semantically rich metadata over your structured data, such as database tables, so you can accomplish complex analytical use cases with natural language. Lastly, a connector links AWS Quick to an external application or a native tool, so agents can read data and take action on your behalf. Cloud connectors connect Quick to services such as Microsoft Outlook, Slack, Jira, Asana, and Salesforce, and to remotely hosted Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. They’re available on every device where you use Quick. Local connectors run on your own machine, such as an MCP server that you host yourself, so their tools are available only when that machine is on and connected. For the full list of connector types, see Connectors and Integration-specific guides in the AWS Quick User Guide. Together, these make your data, documents, and applications available through natural language, so you can ask questions and take actions in your connected sources. A skill is a reusable set of instructions that teaches an agent how to do a specific task. Skills are also the foundation of how an agent in Quick behaves and completes work. Like other agents, an agent in Quick runs in a harness (a managed agent loop) that follows the reasoning and acting (ReAct) pattern. When you supply AWS Quick with a prompt, the agent uses its available tools and instructions to accomplish its goal and supply you with a response. Agent frameworks such as the Strands Agents SDK are built around the same model-driven loop. Much of what Quick does by default comes from system skills . For example, you can ask Quick to generate a Word document, a PowerPoint presentation, an Excel spreadsheet, or a PDF. A system skill can then create or edit the document using code with scripts the skill bundles. Other system skills browse the web, run code, execute deep research, transcribe audio and video, and generate images. Some manage Quick itself, such as building AWS Quick Flows , scheduling routines, handing work to a coding agent such as Kiro, managing your memories and knowledge graph, or tracking your to-dos. Within Quick, you can turn system skills on or off, but you can’t edit, duplicate, export, publish, share, or delete them. Skills can do many kinds of work because of the capabilities and tools that AWS Quick supplies. For example, one skill can produce a deliverable, such as a weekly status update built from your template. Another can automate a workflow across your connectors, such as gathering the week’s Jira updates and posting a summary to Slack. A skill can also run calculations in Python scripts and chart the results with JavaScript. Quick skills follow the Agent Skills specification, which Anthropic originally developed and released as an open standard. AWS Quick on desktop, which launched in preview in April 2026 and became generally available in September 2026 , uses this specification. A skill is a folder with a Markdown file SKILL.md at its root, plus any optional scripts or other reference files its instructions use. The file’s frontmatter, the attributes between two --- lines, holds the name, description, and any other metadata relevant to your skill. See the following shortened example of a skill named release-notes-generator . The description and name are the two most important aspects to triggering a skill. Quick uses progressive disclosure when it loads your skills into the agent’s prompt. The agent reads only each skill’s name and description until a request calls for that skill. It then loads the skill’s full instructions, as How agents load skills describes. This means certain phrases can help trigger the skill, such as “generate my release notes for version 2.3.” The specification caps name at 64 characters and description at 1,024, and recommends instructions within the skill to be under 5,000 tokens. Figure 2: The release-notes-generator skill folder, with a required SKILL.

title: Single-shot and agentic retrieval with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base
abstract: A banking operations employee starts the morning by asking an internal AI assistant which documents are needed to open a business account. The answer is in a single checklist. A few hours later, the same employee asks how those requirements differ across sole proprietorships, LLCs, and partnerships with multiple owners. That answer is spread across several policy guides. One assistant has to handle both questions, quickly and cheaply for the first and thoroughly for the second. Applications need a way to match retrieval effort to each request without building separate systems for simple and complex questions. Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base now supports single-shot Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) and retrieval-only requests through AgenticRetrieveStream . With single-shot RAG, the service searches your knowledge bases once and uses a foundation model (FM) to generate an answer from the passages it finds. With retrieval-only requests, the service returns the matching passages without generating an answer, so your application or the user can work with the source text directly. These modes join the existing agentic retrieval, where the service plans and runs multiple searches before answering. You can now use the same API for both of the employee’s questions: single-shot RAG for the checklist lookup and agentic retrieval for the cross-policy comparison. In this post, we explain how the new settings work and when to use each mode. We use an illustrative internal banking policy assistant to show how single-shot RAG handles direct questions and how agentic retrieval supports comparisons across policy documents. We also show how to configure retrieval-only requests when an employee needs to review source passages rather than a generated answer. Agentic retrieval helps an assistant answer questions that require more than one search. A foundation model breaks the question into sub-queries, searches the relevant knowledge bases, and evaluates whether the results provide enough information to answer the original question. If it identifies gaps, it can refine the search and retrieve additional evidence, within the configured iteration limit. For application builders, this provides several benefits: These agentic capabilities remain valuable for complex questions. For straightforward lookups, applications also need a way to retrieve and answer without additional planning. The expanded maxAgentIteration range closes that gap. With one parameter, you can choose one of three modes for each request: Single-shot RAG uses one foundation model call to generate the answer, which can reduce latency and model usage compared with agentic retrieval. Retrieval-only requests make no foundation model calls. You can balance speed and answer quality for each request, without integrating a second API or maintaining separate code paths for simple and complex queries. Before walking through the new values, it helps to anchor on how iterations are counted, because that is what makes the behavior predictable. One iteration equals one foundation model call. The loop always ends with a single answer-generation call. A value of n buys up to n minus 1 agentic planning rounds, with the last iteration reserved for generating the response. Each planning round is one query rewrite plus a retrieval. More iterations means more planning rounds and better results on hard questions. Fewer iterations means lower latency. One thing that doesn’t count: speculative retrieval. The initial retrieval that runs ahead of the first planning step is retrieval, not an iteration. It never counts against your maxAgentIteration value, and it only ever makes a request faster. Keep that distinction in mind as you read the following values. All three modes support multiple knowledge bases, including maxAgentIteration=0 and 1 . Single-shot retrieval doesn’t mean a single knowledge base. Agentic mode adds query decomposition, evidence evaluation, and iterative searches, rather than exclusive access to multiple knowledge bases. This is single-shot RAG: one retrieval, then one answer. No agentic planning, no query rewriting. The API retrieves once against your query and generates a response grounded in those passages. This is the retrieve once, then generate a response pattern that previously wasn’t expressible through this API. Pair it with generateResponse=true to get a generated answer grounded in the retrieved passages. If you only need the passages, use maxAgentIteration=0 instead, as described in the next section. If most of your traffic is well-scoped, direct questions, this is likely the setting you want as a default. This runs one guaranteed retrieval and generates nothing. No foundation model is invoked. It is equivalent to calling the Retrieve API directly. This makes it most useful for callers who are already standardized on AgenticRetrieveStream and would rather change a parameter than switch APIs. Because no large language model (LLM) is called, there is no answer to generate. Setting generateResponse=true at this value is invalid and returns a 4xx error, because generating an answer requires an LLM call. In agentic mode , a foundation model breaks complex questions into focused sub-queries and retrieves evidence in multiple steps, including across multiple knowledge bases. It evaluates the retrieved information and can refine its searches when evidence is missing. This approach can improve retrieval accuracy for multi-part and comparative questions that a single search might not fully address. With response generation enabled, a value of n allows up to n minus 1 planning rounds before generating an answer grounded in the retrieved evidence. Existing requests using values from 2–5 retain their current behavior. The lower the value, the faster and more predictable the call. The higher the value, the more the planner can decompose and refine on genuinely hard questions. Start low for simple traffic, raise it when accuracy on complex queries matters more than latency. Consider a fictional bank whose operations team uses an internal assistant backed by a knowledge base of account-opening procedures, documentation checklists, and policy guides. Employees use the assistant to locate and understand the bank’s documented requirements. The following examples illustrate how the application can select a retrieval mode for each workflow. They don’t describe a customer deployment or measured results. The following diagram shows how the banking assistant selects a retrieval mode for each request. Figure 1: How the banking assistant selects a retrieval mode for each request An employee asks the assistant a question. The application chooses a retrieval mode and sends the request to AgenticRetrieveStream . With single-shot RAG, the service searches the knowledge base once and generates an answer. With agentic retrieval, the service splits the question into parts, searches several times, and then generates an answer with citations. With retrieval-only, the service returns source passages without generating an answer. The following sections explain each mode. An employee asks, “What documents are required to open a business checking account for a sole proprietor?” In this example, the bank maintains a dedicated checklist that contains the answer. The application sets maxAgentIteration=1 and generateResponse=true to retrieve relevant passages and generate a response, without query rewriting or agentic planning. This is the single-shot RAG pattern: one retrieval, followed by one answer-generation call. It avoids a planning step when the question and supporting content are already well scoped. Another employee asks, “How do account-opening requirements differ for sole proprietors and LLCs, and what additional checks, if any, apply to nonresident owners under our policy?” Answering this question might require information from separate procedures and ownership-verification guides.

title: Introducing Claude Fable 5.2 on AWS
abstract: Today, we are announcing the availability of Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 on Amazon Bedrock and Claude Platform on AWS. Claude Fable 5.2 is Anthropic’s most capable generally available model for technical work that raises the bar in coding and the sciences. Claude Mythos 5.2 is available through Anthropic’s verification programs for advanced work in cyber security and life sciences. In this post, we cover what’s new in both models, why Fable 5.2 matters for your technical workloads, and how to get started building with the model on Amazon Bedrock. Fable 5.2 raises the bar on the hardest problems in coding, math, and science. It takes on ambiguous, multi-step work, verifies its own output, and can run unattended for hours to days. It interprets prompts, iterates, catches its own errors, and optimizes as it goes. In Anthropic’s alignment testing, Mythos 5.2 hallucinates less, completes tasks more reliably, surfaces important information more consistently, and self-reports issues more honestly than Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Mythos 5.1. Anthropic expects Fable 5.2 to behave similarly. If a cyber security query is declined, you can retry it on Opus 4.8, and if a biology query is declined, you can retry it on Opus 5. On Amazon Bedrock, the retry is your code’s job, not an automatic switch. If the declined request hit the prompt cache, the refusal also includes a fallback credit token. Send that token with the retry and it’s billed as cache reads, so you don’t pay to write the same cache twice. Check the documentation for more information on fallback credit. For authorized work in cyber security and life sciences, Claude Mythos 5.2 is available through Anthropic’s verification programs . Mythos 5.2 covers two high-risk domains, available only through the verification programs noted earlier: Anthropic designates Claude Fable 5.2 as a Covered Model . By default, its use requires retention for up to 30 days and human safety review. On Amazon Bedrock, Amazon personnel perform the review within the AWS boundary. Set the aws_review data retention mode on your account or project before you invoke the model. See Amazon Bedrock data retention for more details. Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS), built in collaboration with AWS, combines the privacy of zero data retention (ZDR) with the latest safeguards for detecting misuse. EFS is available now. A version that keeps your data in a bucket and under keys you control is expected to follow, and it has not launched yet. Until it does, eligible customers can use Fable 5.2 with zero data retention through June 30, 2027. To try Fable 5.2, open the Amazon Bedrock console , choose Test , Playground , and select Fable 5.2 as the model. From there, you can run a prompt directly against it. Programmatically, you can call the model with the Anthropic Messages API against bedrock-runtime (through the Anthropic SDK). You can also stay on the Invoke and Converse APIs on bedrock-runtime through the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) and AWS SDK . To follow along with the code examples in this post, you need the following: Here’s a quick example using the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3): You can explore the Getting Started notebook for more examples. For teams already running Claude models on Amazon Bedrock, the claude-api skill in Claude Code helps you upgrade to Fable 5.2. The claude-api skill is an open-source skill built into Claude Code that captures the details that make Claude API code work well. It covers which agent patterns fit a given job, what parameters change between model generations, and when to apply prompt caching. It stays current as Anthropic’s SDKs evolve: when a new model is released or the API gains a feature, the skill already knows. When you ask Claude Code to upgrade your codebase to Fable 5.2, the skill reviews your code and walks you through: The skill also detects your deployment platform including Amazon Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, and other environments and adjusts model ID formats and feature configurations accordingly. For example, it uses the Amazon Bedrock structured model ID format ( global.anthropic.claude-fable-5-2 ). In Claude Code, run the migration directly: This scans your working directory (or a subdirectory or specific file list you confirm) and applies the migration changes in a single guided pass. You can also invoke it conversationally by telling Claude Code: The claude-api skill is available in Claude Code and is also bundled into CodeRabbit, JetBrains IDEs (including Junie), Resolve AI, and Warp. It is open source at anthropics/skills on GitHub, so any coding agent can integrate it. Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 are available today on Amazon Bedrock through US Geo CRIS and Global CRIS inference profiles. See the Bedrock documentation for the full list of supported Regions. For pricing information, see Amazon Bedrock pricing . Both models are also available through Claude Platform on AWS in every Region where the service is offered. Give Claude Fable 5.2 a try in the Amazon Bedrock console , in Claude Platform on AWS , or explore the Getting Started notebook on GitHub.

title: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
abstract: Today, we’re announcing that NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. You can deploy it with a few steps in SageMaker Studio or with a few lines of the SageMaker Python SDK. Super VL is the vision-language model (VLM) in the NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 family. It accepts images, video, and text as input and generates text. The model pairs a 120B-parameter hybrid Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language backbone with 12B active parameters and a C-RADIO vision encoder. It supports context lengths of up to 1 million tokens and includes a built-in Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) head that supports speculative decoding. You can configure reasoning per request. NVIDIA built Super VL for document intelligence, GUI understanding for computer-use agents, video question answering, and multimodal agentic applications. JumpStart offers two variants: NVFP4, quantized from BF16 with quantization-aware distillation for optimized inference, and the BF16 full-precision reference weights. In this post, we walk through the model’s capabilities and the JumpStart deployment configurations. We then show the measured inference performance and demonstrate text, image, and video inference. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is a 120B-parameter model with 12B active parameters per token. It combines a hybrid language backbone with a dedicated vision encoder. The following table compares the specifications of the two variants available in JumpStart. Super VL is aimed at agentic workloads that must see and read. It targets vision-language agents that combine reasoning, coding, tool use, document understanding, and video understanding. The NVIDIA model cards report results for both checkpoints across reasoning, coding, agentic, long-context, and multimodal benchmarks, with evaluation settings held constant so that only the checkpoint differs. The following table highlights the multimodal benchmarks most relevant to vision-language workloads (reasoning on). NVFP4, the JumpStart default, matches BF16 on MMLongBench-Doc and stays within about one point on the others, scoring slightly higher on OCRBench v2 and OSWorld-Verified. For the full comparison against other publicly available models and the evaluation settings, see the NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL and Lightning Technical Report . We measured inference performance with the JumpStart release container using the generate workload profile: 250 input tokens, 1,500 output tokens, and five concurrent streaming requests. Throughput is the mean output tokens per second for each request, and time to first token is the mean across requests. These results illustrate the deployment choices available through JumpStart. The NVFP4 variant runs on G7 instances with a smaller GPU footprint. The BF16 variant on ml.p5en.48xlarge achieved 140.85 output tokens per second per request in this test. Time to first token remained about half a second across all three configurations. Because the variants run on different GPU systems and configurations, these measurements are not an isolated BF16-versus-NVFP4 precision comparison. Longer prompts change the picture: with the summarize profile (10,000 input tokens), time to first token on ml.g7.24xlarge is 12.62 seconds. SageMaker JumpStart supports Nemotron 3.5 Super VL on the following validated instance types. NVFP4 runs on G7 instances with NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs, and BF16 runs on P5en instances with NVIDIA H200 GPUs. The JumpStart default instance for NVFP4 is ml.g7.24xlarge, which serves as the recommended starting point for the generate profile. The checkpoint includes the MTP head, but the JumpStart serving configuration does not enable speculative decoding. You can deploy the model from SageMaker Studio, with the SageMaker Python SDK, or from the Hugging Face model page. Before you deploy, make sure you have the following: To deploy the model from SageMaker Studio, complete the following steps: Figure 1: Searching for NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL in SageMaker JumpStart Figure 2: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL NVFP4 model card in SageMaker JumpStart Choose BF16 if you need the full-precision reference weights on ml.p5en.48xlarge. The following screenshot shows the BF16 model card. Figure 3: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL BF16 model card in SageMaker JumpStart Figure 4: Reviewing Nemotron 3.5 Super VL capabilities and model details before deployment Figure 5: SageMaker endpoint deployment in progress before the status reaches InService The example uses the SageMaker Python SDK v3 classes: JumpStartConfig names the model, ModelBuilder builds and deploys it, and deploy returns an Endpoint resource. Pass the instance type in Compute , because the SDK falls back to ml.m5.large when the instance type is absent, and the build then fails. The deploy call waits until the endpoint is InService, which takes about 10 minutes on ml.g7.24xlarge. The inference_config_name argument selects a serving configuration, and each configuration sets a different context length. The default generate configurations serve a 2,275-token context sized for short prompts. The summarize configurations serve 13,650 tokens, and the modify configurations serve 15,600 tokens. The example uses a modify configuration because the inference examples in this post, especially image, video, and reasoning requests, need the larger context. All the inference examples that follow assume the modify configuration. You can also deploy the model from its Hugging Face model page: choose Deploy , then Amazon SageMaker AI , and continue to the SageMaker deployment workflow. Figure 6: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL model page on Hugging Face with the Deploy menu On the deployment menu, choose Amazon SageMaker AI to open the SageMaker deployment workflow, as shown in the following screenshot. Figure 7: Selecting Amazon SageMaker AI from the Hugging Face deployment workflow After the endpoint is InService, you can send inference requests to it. The JumpStart endpoint exposes a vLLM-powered chat completions API, so applications can send inference requests using a familiar chat-message format. NVIDIA recommends temperature 1.0 and top_p 0.95 for text, and temperature 0.6 and top_p 0.95 for image and video requests. You must send media inline as base64 data URLs because the endpoint runs with network isolation and cannot fetch URLs. Reasoning is on by default, and you can configure it per request. The reasoning text is returned in the reasoning field of the message, separate from content. For direct extraction-style tasks, you can disable reasoning with enable_thinking=False in chat_template_kwargs . The model accepts images rather than raw PDF files. To process a PDF, render each page to an image such as PNG before sending it to the model. A 1,536 x 1,024 page costs about 1,536 tokens of context, and one request can carry one image. The following example sends a short MP4 clip as a base64-encoded data URL and asks the model to summarize it, with reasoning disabled for a direct response. For video inference, use short, compressed clips and keep the encoded request within the endpoint’s supported payload limits. For reasoning-intensive video requests, set max_tokens high enough to allow the model to complete its reasoning while considering response length and endpoint invocation limits. Consider the following recommendations when you run Nemotron 3.5 Super VL on SageMaker JumpStart: To avoid ongoing charges, delete the endpoint, the endpoint configuration, and the model when you are done: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL brings image, video, and document understanding to SageMaker JumpStart. The NVFP4 variant is available on G7 instances with NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs. The BF16 variant is available on ml.p5en.48xlarge with NVIDIA H200 GPUs. Choose NVFP4 for optimized inference with model quality close to the BF16 checkpoint, or BF16 when you want the full-precision reference weights.

title: Pluggable Agentic AI Framework: A seven-layer composable enterprise agentic AI reference architecture on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: “How do we run our AI agents in production at scale?” is the question every customer eventually asks. It comes bundled with several questions. How do we handle thousands of concurrent user requests securely and confidently? How do we make sure the agents stay reliable under real traffic instead of failing silently? How do we know if an agent still meets the quality and safety standards it passed during testing? What are agent security best practices? Should that be deterministic or non-deterministic? And many more. A proof-of-concept answers none of these, because it is built to show the agent model can do the task, not to survive production traffic, cost pressure, and security review. That gap between a working prototype and a system that runs reliably, securely, frugally and responsibly at scale, is where most agentic AI initiatives stall, and it is rarely the model’s fault. Every team building an agent tends to rebuild the same scaffolding from scratch: its own routing logic, its own guardrails, its own observability, all applied after the fact rather than built in from the start. The teams need a shared, production-ready architecture that every agent can build on. This post walks through a seven-layer composable reference architecture designed to take multi-agent AI applications from prototype to production scale. The Pluggable Agentic AI Framework is a reference architecture for multi-agent applications organized into seven layers , each with a distinct responsibility and a stable contract. The services and technologies shown in each layer reflect the reference implementation, not mandatory choices. Organizations can substitute alternatives that align with their existing infrastructure and requirements. Together, these layers offer a blueprint for building, securing, and operating agentic AI applications at production scale. Figure 1: The seven layers of the Pluggable Agentic AI Framework Data and Knowledge is the foundation of Agentic AI. An agent is only as good as the data it can access. Whether an agent is checking out a healthcare formulary, tracking inventory, or interpreting a compliance rule, it needs relevant, up-to-date information to answer correctly. This layer owns retrieval, embeddings, and access to structured and unstructured data through a clear contract and protocol: accept a query and return the most relevant information that acts as context for an agent. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base , Vector Engine for Amazon OpenSearch Serverless , Amazon S3 Vectors and Amazon DynamoDB are example building blocks for this foundation. Model and Inference choices should be driven by configuration, not hardwired into agent or application logic. Use smaller, faster models for simple tasks and larger models for requests that require more nuanced reasoning. It is important to conduct a thorough model evaluation for the use case you are building with realistic and representative business data. A model routing layer keeps AI agents decoupled from the model hosting environment and provider-specific APIs by relying on a consistent request-and-response contract. A proxy such as LiteLLM provides a common interface across providers, so you can switch models based on your evaluations without rewriting application logic. Orchestration determines how work is distributed, and choosing the right approach is critical. For straightforward tasks, use a single agent to handle the work from end to end. For complex, cross-domain workflows, use a supervisor to delegate specialist agents, each scoped to a specific capability and tied to a specific set of tools. Avoid building one agent that does everything. As tools, instructions, and context accumulate, the context window grows, latency increases, and accuracy can suffer. Tool sprawl sets in, which can push agents beyond their intended boundaries, leading to unintended actions and security breaches. Splitting responsibilities keeps each agent’s context focused and makes latency more predictable. You can also test each agent’s behavior, scale it, and define its security model independently. Enforce bounded autonomy: specialists should execute strictly within the tools they have been granted, and nothing more. In addition to decomposing into specific specialists and setting its boundary, decouple the specialist agents from the supervisor agents. Allow the supervisor to discover the specialists from a centralized agent registry and invoke them through a standardized protocol like MCP (Model Context Protocol) and A2A (Agent to Agent). Maintain a centralized agent registry that catalogs every agent’s tools, skills, and owner. This gives your organization the visibility it needs for governance at scale, increases the velocity of AI agent implementation through reusability, and avoids the cost of repetitive development. Consider using Strands Agents for specialists, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness for the orchestrator, AWS Agent Registry and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway for centralized discovery and routing. Security and Guardrails should be a primary concern, built into the design from day one. Agentic AI exposes organizations to a new class of risks that conventional security frameworks were not built to address, from prompt injection and tool misuse to memory and data poisoning. Treat all external content as untrusted by default. Authenticate every request, whether it comes from a user, another agent, or an automated workflow, through a service like Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity . Then use fine-grained access control to determine whether each tool call is permitted before execution. Grant agents temporary, scoped credentials instead of persistent secrets. On the data-protection side, mask sensitive data like PHI (Personal Health Information) and PII (Personally Identifiable Information) in agent and tool requests and responses, so that sensitive customer information does not appear in agent outputs or lingers in memory. For accountability, capture every significant decision in a tamper-evident audit trail, route high-impact actions through a human approval gate, and deploy circuit breakers to halt anomalous behavior before it can escalate. Consider using Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for user inputs, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity and Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for authentication and access control, along with AWS Security and governance controls to bring defense-in-depth security. Application is where the end-user experience lives, whether that is a chat interface, an API surface, or an embedded widget. Keep this layer intentionally thin. Its only responsibilities should be presenting the conversation and passing requests to the orchestration layer beneath it. Resist the urge to embed business logic here. The cleaner the separation, the more easily you can iterate on the user experience without destabilizing the backend. A decision model can sit at this boundary as a fast, inexpensive check: in one call it scores whether a request is in scope, needs a human, or is urgent, returning probabilities instead of free text. Your code acts on those scores with simple thresholds, answering off-topic requests directly and flagging escalations, so the full agentic loop runs only when it adds value. When building the application layer, think about what would be needed for another AI agent to consume and interact with your AI agents along with humans. Build your external interfaces accordingly. Observability should watch every layer from day one, not after the first incident. Along with the logs and metrics, end-to-end agent traces are critical to measure whether the agent performed its task correctly. Along with the trace, collect cost and token usage per request, time to first token, whether the call is secure, and surface dashboards for latency, error rates, and spend before you go live. Proactive monitoring is cheaper than reactive firefighting.

title: How CrossnoKaye grounds physical AI with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: Industrial operations present AI challenges that don’t show up in typical enterprise software. In most facilities, plant data and control logic are spread across separate systems from different vendors: programmable logic controllers (PLCs) and distributed control systems (DCS) run the equipment logic, historians record time-series tags under site-specific naming schemes, supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems drive operator screens, and standalone optimization tools or alarm loggers sit on the side. Bolting an external AI agent onto that stack rarely works well in practice. Each system uses its own naming conventions. The logic that actually governs how equipment behaves (the control sequences, state machines, and safety interlocks) is locked inside proprietary controller code that an external tool can’t inspect. Giving a bolt-on agent access across multiple operational technology (OT) systems also means distributing credentials across the plant network. CrossnoKaye took a different approach to bring physical AI to heavy industry using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore . Its software-defined automation platform, ATLAS, connects live plant data and AI reasoning to closed-loop control of the equipment running food and beverage plants, industrial refrigeration facilities, aggregates quarries, and manufacturing sites. Across more than 100 industrial facilities and 13,000 controlled assets, CrossnoKaye stores over 22 trillion machine data points, ingests more than 50 billion new readings every day, and runs over 1,000 live advanced process control (APC) applications; CrossnoKaye reports that these applications improve production throughput by 11–17 percent while reducing total facility energy costs by an average of 21 percent. Because ATLAS already manages the facility model, the base control software, the historian, and the optimization applications in one platform on AWS, CrossnoKaye’s agentic intelligence system, AURA, has native access to the full operational state of the plant within a single security boundary. Having the plant context is only half the problem, though. Large language models (LLMs) are good at interpreting engineering context and planning an investigation, but they cannot reliably compute statistics or physical balances over millions of sensor readings in a prompt. To back every numerical answer with real math, AURA uses the code interpreter capability in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to write and run Python workloads at runtime inside isolated, AWS managed microVM sandboxes, alongside Amazon Bedrock Guardrails and local edge safety controls. This post covers how CrossnoKaye architected ATLAS and AURA on AWS, how AURA uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore across interactive Chats, repeatable Tasks, and automated Routines, and what the team learned running physical AI in production. ATLAS controls industrial processes across existing PLC and DCS infrastructure, from kilns, crushers, drying rooms, ovens, and spiral freezers to chillers, turbines, valves, and compressors, without requiring customers to rip and replace plant hardware. Figure 1 illustrates how on-premises ATLAS edge clusters, continuous cloud optimization, and AURA work together on AWS. Figure 1: CrossnoKaye AURA and ATLAS physical AI architecture with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore ATLAS and AURA are built around three core layers: First, the plant is defined in software from the edge up. At each facility, an on-premises ATLAS control panel with redundant computers, power supplies, and network switches (so local control continues uninterrupted while a failed hardware component is replaced) runs a local Kubernetes cluster that uses contract-first microservices, extending the ATLAS cloud platform on AWS to the plant floor. In the cloud, ATLAS authors, validates, and versions the facility’s base control narratives (defining equipment state machines, sequences, operating bounds, interlocks, and alarm rules), which are downloaded to the edge appliances and run locally against existing equipment and controllers. CrossnoKaye reports over 9,000 control software deployments per year and more than 1 million run hours with zero safety incidents. Each edge appliance also acts as an outbound-only information technology/operational technology (IT/OT) gateway that opens zero inbound firewall ports inside the plant, streaming high-frequency telemetry to AWS through Amazon VPC Lattice and Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (Amazon MSK) . If cloud connectivity drops, the plant continues running safely on the base control narratives on the local edge cluster. Second, derived engineering signals and closed-loop optimization applications run on top of base control using the same shared plant model. In the cloud, CrossnoKaye’s Scheduling system runs two continuous pipelines from versioned Python packages in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) , operating on configurable per-instance cadences and event-driven triggers when plant settings change. Synthetic reading algorithms compute derived engineering metrics, such as heat-flow distributions, asset health indices, energy intensity, and mass-balance deviations, and write them back to the historian alongside physical I/O. Closed-loop optimization applications run on top of the base control layer, combining those derived synthetic readings with physics models, model predictive control (MPC), reinforcement learning, utility tariffs, and weather forecasts to compute optimal setpoint schedules. Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queues order every schedule and state update by facility before dispatching setpoints to the local base control narrative on the edge cluster, which CrossnoKaye reports runs 650,000 closed-loop control actions per day. Third, AURA runs inside the platform boundary on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) as microservices and durable Temporal workflows. Under the caller’s enterprise permissions, AURA agents query the internal Atlas Data gateway to read the operational state of a facility or fleet in one consistent model: upstream and downstream equipment topology, the deployed base control narratives and interlocks, physical I/O and synthetic readings, setting change and alarm histories, active optimization schedules, and plant documentation indexed in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases . Having the equipment layout, the base control logic, and the sensor data in the same system makes a concrete difference when diagnosing plant issues. At an aggregates quarry running primary, secondary, and tertiary rock crushers, the back half of the plant tripped twice in a single shift. From the control room, operators saw the secondary crusher fault, cleared the alarm, and restarted the line, only for it to trip again hours later. In the historian timestamps alone, the secondary crusher faulted seconds after the tertiary crusher, which made it look like a crusher problem. Because AURA also reads the conveyor layout and the deployed base control interlocks, its investigation followed the actual control logic. A recirculating belt beneath the tertiary crusher was slipping, which tripped the tertiary crusher’s overload interlock. That interlock’s upstream safety interlock immediately halted the secondary crusher to prevent burying a stopped downstream crusher in stone. Instead of chasing a phantom crusher fault, the plant manager sent an operator to inspect the recirculating belt, confirming and fixing the slip in minutes. The numbered flows in Figure 1 trace how an AURA investigation runs on AWS: AURA combines foundation models on Amazon Bedrock (for model availability by AWS Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide) with isolated Python sandboxes in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Code Interpreter, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, across three operational modes: The following sections examine four architectural decisions behind these workflows.

title: Professional work deserves professional tools. Meet AWS Quick.
abstract: Our first brand campaign celebrates teams who keep business moving and the AI workspace built only for them. Every day, teams at leading enterprises use AWS Quick to research, analyze, and act across the data and applications they already rely on. Today we’re launching our first brand campaign to bring that same experience to millions more knowledge workers around the world. The campaign runs across the United States and the United Kingdom on streaming TV, online video, social media, and leading business publications. AWS Quick is the AI workspace built only for work, where teams use AI agents to research, analyze, and act across the data and applications they already rely on. Across virtually every industry, leading enterprises including 3M, BMW, Mondelez, New York Life, and Southwest Airlines are using Quick to transform how they work. The campaign celebrates the teams who know that the work they do every day deserves tools built for it. Customers tell us their AI assistants make individuals faster, but the gains stay personal. A sales rep still builds territory plans by pulling from the CRM, dashboards, call notes, and email. Because context stays locked inside a single project or one vendor’s suite, productivity never compounds across the team or the company. Most of those tools started as consumer apps and still serve personal and professional use with the same product. AWS Quick took the opposite path: it was built for work from day one, on the same AWS infrastructure that millions of customers use to run their mission-critical applications. These include many of the world’s most complex and security-sensitive workloads. AWS Quick has no consumer version. Every roadmap decision and every feature we ship starts with one question: does it help individuals, teams, and entire enterprises do their most important work? Quick knows your role, your team, and how your projects, people, and data connect, because it works across the applications and workflows your teams already use. Quick watches for changes, surfaces what matters, and acts on your behalf, which leaves your team free to focus on what moves the business forward. Anyone can build agents, apps, and automations by describing what they need in plain language, without filing an IT ticket. Everything built in a shared space becomes an asset the whole team can use. Quick is integrated with the security and compliance tools you already use, including Microsoft Purview for data protection, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), and Microsoft Active Directory for permission-based controls. Quick reads the sensitivity labels already on your files, enforces existing permissions, and flags potentially sensitive data to administrators. Assets including agents, knowledge bases, and skills reach new teams only through approved sharing, and every approval and denial is recorded with who decided, what they shared, and why. Quick also carries the compliance certifications most organizations require, including HIPAA, FedRAMP, SOC 2, and ISO 27001. Your data is yours, and your conversations are private. No one else can browse your conversations, and IT admins cannot access your chat transcripts. Amazon CloudWatch and AWS CloudTrail are built in, giving your organization a full audit trail of what happened, who did it, and when. Your data never leaves your environment and never trains someone else’s models. That commitment is also why we’re now AWS Quick, a name that signals the enterprise security and governance that have been part of Quick from the start. IT leaders, account executives, program managers, and finance leads all work differently, and Quick works the way each of them does, on any device and on their schedule. You bring the judgment, and Quick gives your team the capacity to match its goals. Ready to transform how your users, teams, and entire enterprise do their best work with an AI built for business? You can download Quick today and get started in minutes , or talk to your AWS account team about options for enterprise pricing plans.

title: Import AI 480: Self-sustaining space economies; AI for science progress, and Meta builds perfect hands for a superintelligence
abstract: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. AI Science startup converts a quantum conjecture into a theorem: …An evocative taste of the singularity… In the same way a few years ago it went from remarkable to unremarkable to see computers gain the ability to identify objects in images, we’re now in an era where it’s rapidly going from remarkable to unremarkable for computers to extend the bounds of human knowledge. The latest example comes from Physical Superintelligence, an AI science startup which has proved a longstanding quantum computing conjecture. What they did: “Open since 2008, the conjecture of Scott Aaronson and Andris Ambainis concerns when quantum computers can be exponentially faster than ordinary ones. Now, a research system developed internally at Physical Superintelligence (PSI), running a non-public Anthropic model, found a proof for it, settling one of the most fundamental questions in quantum computing,” the startup writes. “The system had a complete proof of the conjecture during the third day of the run, and Lean, a proof assistant in which a computer checks every step, accepted it. We then set the system to work on related open problems. Along the way, the system improved the result twice, and Lean accepted the final version.” Why this matters – we are in the singularity : As I said in my speech at the IMF ( #477 ), I believe we’re in the early stages of the singularity, defined as the period when the rate of technological and scientific progress exceeds the rate at which we humans can parse out and make sense of it. Research like this is a taste of what that means; mostly automated synthetic researchers extending the frontier of knowledge, spitting out results which need to then be understood by humans. Read more: A proof of the Aaronson‑Ambainis conjecture (Physical Superintelligence, blog) . Meta builds the hands that a superintelligence needs to take over the world: …Combine Tactus with an autonomous agent and you have the makings of a scifi takeover… Meta Reality Labs Research has published details on Tactus, “a textile-integrated tactile and pose sensing glove designed from the ground up for naturalistic manipulation data collection”. The cool thing about this glove is that it helps record fine-grained detail from hands as they’re manipulating objects – this is the kind of thing that cameras can visually report but often leads to sub-par data due to occlusion during manipulation. It’s also interesting because this is exactly the kind of hardware an autonomous AI system might want to pay humans to wear so it could gather data and get feedback from the world. More details on Tactus: The gloves have three design pillars: “(1) a thin, conformal 3D-knit form factor (1.5mm fingertip stackup) designed to minimize interference with natural manipulation, (2) strategically placed capacitive tactile sensors at manipulation-relevant regions informed by empirical contact studies”, Meta writes. “Tactus provides calibrated fingertip force sensing and occlusion-resilient hand tracking in a textile-integrated form factor that preserves natural grasp behavior.” “(3) IMU-fused pose tracking that maintains accuracy through the hand-object occlusions where manipulation data is most valuable.” Why this matters – hand-by-wire: Picture some takeoff scenario where an AI system has carved out an independent niche for itself running on some stolen compute, perhaps even using a form of distributed inference and training. The AI now has a few goals, some of which can be satisfied by doing things in the digital world, and some of which can be satisfied by doing things in the physical world. For the physical world stuff, it either needs to be able to get robots to do the thing, or figure out a way to get people to work for it – the Tactus gloves are the kind of hardware you might imagine a rogue AI paying people to wear so they could both a) perform tasks for it and it could give live feedback, and b) become a source of data generation for the AI itself. Of course, I am not endorsing this particular future! But I have begun to find it helpful to view research papers through the lens of “how would an AI use this”, similar to how it is often helpful to view papers through the lens of “how would an intelligence agency use the insights shared here”. Read more : Tactus: Tactile & Pose Sensing Glove for Natural Dexterity Data Collection (arXiv) . Building a self-sustaining space economy is cheaper than you think – especially with Starship: …A 2016 NASA paper contains some exciting ideas for off-Earth industrialization… Here’s a fascinating paper from researchers with the NASA Kennedy Space Center in 2016 about what it’d take to bootstrap a self-sustaining industry on the moon. “Once successfully bootstrapped, a robotic network can access, process, transport, and utilize the solar system’s resources for mankind’s benefit,” the researchers write. Moon manufacturing – cheaper than you think: The big idea in the paper is how little mass is required to kickstart a manufacturing ecosystem. The key is to start with a relatively basic set of things and then build up from there, eventually fabricating chips on the moon. “In the baseline case with maximum manufacturing rate, a total of 41 MT is launched to the Moon. In the reduced rate case, only 12 MT is launched to the Moon but the scale of industry is two orders of magnitude smaller so the benefits of the industry are relatively delayed by eight years”. Starship has a capacity to lift 100 MT to low-earth orbit, and given multiple refuelings in orbit it’s feasible you could then land it on the moon – when you napkin out the cost of multiple Starship launches and refuelings you can get 12-41MT to the Moon for between $1.5bn and $4.2bn at list prices. What you build on the moon and in what order: The basic idea here is to start by building simple things and then move up from there by launching a “sub-replicating system and evolve it toward the self-replication capability,” they write. “The objective is for the first robotic “colonists” on the Moon to fabricate a set of, say, 1700’s era machines and then to advance them steadily through the equivalent of the 1800’s, 1900’s, and finally back into the 2000’s. We argue that this can be accomplished in just a few decades”. The authors see this unfolding over 6 distinct manufacturing generations: Gen 1: Making gases, water, crude alloys, ceramics, solar cells. Gen 2.5: Plastics, rubbers, some chemicals. Gen 3 : Diversify chemicals, simple fabrics, eventually polymers. Gen 4: Sandwiched and other advanced material processes. Gen 5: Large-scale production. Gen 6: Makes all necessary materials, increasing sophistication, including making all electronics locally. What machines do you send to the moon? Excavators: “travel between the digging site and the resource processing site, delivering sufficient lunar regolith each hour to maintain production rates of the other assets.” Chemical plants for volatiles : One type will be oriented around producing gases and liquids like oxygen, hydrogen, water, hydrocarbons like methane, and solvents for industrial processes. Chemical plants for solids: Produce plastics and rubbers from lunar pole ice. “We now know that the ice contains large quantities of carbon molecules (CO, CO2,…) as well as nitrogen-bearing and hydrogen-bearing molecules… these materials may be needed for gaskets, seals, and insulators, for example.” Metal and Ceramics refining: Early generations will “produce crude ‘mongrel alloys’ by electrowinning or other methods” and hardware built out of this stuff will need to be huge to add strength to make up for poor mechanical properties. “Subsequent generations of metal refineries will add processes and material streams to improve the mechanics of the materials.

title: “AI毀了我的計算機學位”
abstract: “AI毀了我的計算機學位” Jay 2026-11-09 16:57:20 來源： 量子位 教授也用Claude糊弄… Jay 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號 QbitAI AI正在毀掉我的計算機學位。 寫下這行控訴的，是一個從小夢想學計算機的大二女生， Katie 。 沒有名校光環，高中數學只拿了個B；此前也沒接受過任何科班集訓，唯一拿得出手的「專案經歷」，不過是幾個略顯簡陋的網頁小遊戲。 原本以為，邁進大學象牙塔，終於能好好學計算機了！ 誰曾想—— 課程大綱是Claude批次生成的，期末大作業是LLM自動批改的，就連導師發來的關懷郵件，很可能也是後臺自動化指令碼。。。 面對這荒誕的一幕，她癱軟了 （bushi） ： 由於AI，我的大學似乎正在經歷一場生死存亡的危機。 部落格釋出不到24小時， 光速成Hacker News首頁熱榜第一 。 徹底崩壞的計算機系 在她的求學經歷裡，自打這波生成式AI爆發後，學校的教學政策就沒停止過反覆橫跳。 最開始當然是全面擁抱： 給學生作業打分寫評語、生成課程大綱、發全員催學郵件……全給安排上了大模型。 結果呢？ 折騰不到三個月，發現全是幻覺與垃圾內容， 光速撤回 。 整套教學管理，始終處於一種極其精神分裂的狀態—— 你們絕對不能使用AI！ 哦不，說錯了，所有人必須使用AI！ 不對不對……好像還是不能用AI啊…… 然後就會出現一個很魔幻的事。 同一門課程，上一個模組的作業，教授強制要求你用AI，說這是這門課成績的重要考核維度。 聽罷，你咬咬牙，自掏腰包開通了Claude訂閱。 到了下一個模組，你滿懷自信地上傳了站起來蹬Opus 5.5調教出來的程式碼，結果—— 不er? 什麼叫學術不端，使用LLM要扣分？？？ 但說實話，如果只是規則朝令夕改，也還好，可以勉強應付。 最讓作者破防的是，自己努力學習考上大學，付這麼高的學費，就是指望能跟著專家教授系統學習。 結果， 你個大學教授也拿Claude糊弄我？？？ 是的，講臺上的導師一邊嚴厲警告學生不要投機取巧，轉過頭自己直接把需求丟給Claude，一鍵生成教學資料。 以前的作業，好歹是教授結合教學目標深思熟慮、在教研組過過一遍的。任務體量適中，循序漸進。 現在？妹子懷疑這幫教授連MD都沒開啟過。 滿篇都是大模型生成的廢話。3000字作業說明，要提交15份材料。 掐指一算， 作業量比以前翻了三倍…… 結果就是，那些本來數學底子就薄、轉專業跨考過來的普通學生，只能被逼著去走馬觀花地速通知識點。 我來這裡是為了踏踏實實學真東西的，該死的，不是為了在一份3000字的作業裡對著15個根本完不成的任務浮於表面！ 但這還不是最崩潰的。 很多同學辛辛苦苦研究了十幾天，但不知道為啥，就是怎麼也跑不通。 結果在DDL前一週，老師突然發了一封 勘誤郵件 ： 大綱裡有兩個地方寫錯了，現已修正，請大家重新提交。 你還我白燒的這麼多Token😭 所以，到底為什麼要這麼幹？ Katie表示， 倒也不能全怪教授們。 罪魁禍首還是管理層。 你知道資方最喜歡聽什麼嗎？規模化學習，最好是自動化的！ 這樣，他們就可以在不支付額外員工費用的情況下，儘可能多地從學費中榨取利潤。 既然大模型能自動化出題，能秒批作業，那為什麼還要花大價錢去聘請助教、增加講師編制？ 技術成了校方無限度削減教學支出的藉口，無止境地壓榨講師，工作量多到光靠人的注意力根本完成。 Katie也提到，自己平時根本見不著導師的影子。 唯一的聯絡是，她在好幾天沒登入線上學習平臺時，會收到一封導師的來信—— 結果滿懷緊張地開啟一看，原來不是導師本人寫的，這玩意兒是觸發的 自動警報 o (╥﹏╥) o。 Hacker News最熱門 帖子釋出後，很快火爆全網，迅速登上Hacker News首頁榜一。 評論區也湧入了很多計算機老哥。 但出乎我意料的是，就算同為計算機系，竟然也並不都是共情的聲音。 整個計算機技術社群， 割裂成了兩極 。 一派是早已在行業立足的 資深老鳥 。 在他們的視角下，當下的種種混亂，不過是技術範式演進過程中的短暫陣痛。 我已經從事這一職業超過二十年了，每天都能學到新的東西。在過去幾年裡，隨著人工智慧技術的發展，我的學習速度更快了，也能更深入地瞭解我所工作的系統。 總而言之就是，AI終歸只是一件趁手的工具。只要善用大模型進行蘇格拉底式的循循誘導，當下的學習資源，不知比他們那時候強出多少倍。 人工智慧並不會取代教育和傳統的學習方式。 相反，人工智慧會提升你理解和記憶的能力。對於一個技術思維較強且自學的專業人士來說，我一直渴望的是持續學習下去。 因此，不少經驗豐富的前輩對新一代新人 反而帶著幾分豔羨 ： 成為一名高階工程師，並不真的取決於你從事軟體開發的時間長短。我見過一些非常出色的21歲開發者，他們的程式設計能力甚至能超越那些已經工作20多年的人。 我認為，他們能能表現如此出色的原因，在於他們具備紮實的電腦科學基礎知識。 但這終究是屬於少數人的敘事。 另一端，絕大多數剛畢業的年輕人， 只感到了窒息 。 有跟帖者貼出了一項量化研究結論： 斯坦福大學的研究人員發現，他們去年所預測的初級職員的就業趨勢仍然持續存在且正在擴大。 具體來說，那些從事最易受人工智慧影響行業的22至25歲員工的就業水平，比那些不常面臨人工智慧衝擊的同行低19%。 對此，一些常年參與招聘的從業者也坦率印證了這一現實： 確實，與其花時間培養一個從零起步的應屆生，不如給資深工程師配上頂配的Coding Agent來得高效。 我真的不知道應該給即將畢業的開發者什麼建議。 花費四年青春學計算機，最後連工作都找不到…… 那，CS學位的意義，究竟是什麼？ 找回程式設計的溫度 對於這個問題，我覺得，或許能在Katie那篇部落格，找到答案。 文章最後，她寫下了這麼一段文字： 我才不管電腦科學和數學是不是已經走到頭了！我還是想學！ 好吧，我確實關心自己未來的職業發展，但這也不意味著我想忘掉已經學過的一切，或者停下探索的腳步。 還有那麼多有趣的方向值得探索，有些和AI有關，有些沒有。可鋪天蓋地的標題總在說什麼「軟體工程完了」「不用AI就會被淘汰」之類的，讓人喘不過氣。 難道女孩就不能單純為了好玩學學統計學嗎？ 經歷了這一切後， Katie給出的答案是—— 我可以繼續，但我不會了。這會讓我消化不良。 也許我會回到OpenProcessing上，做一些更愚蠢的遊戲。 至少，現在我真的知道如何做一些程式設計了。 然後，她貼出了自己早年間在OpenProcessing上寫的幾個簡陋小網頁： 一個放著帶感音樂的簡單太空射擊遊戲； 一隻點一下就會「喵」一聲的莫古利； 還有一個用麥克風聲音把小魚嚇跑的互動demo。 實話說，非常粗糙。 任何一個拎出來，都比如今Astra、Fable一句Prompt直出的效果差了十萬八千里。 甚至可能還不如一個新模型的鵜鶘腳踏車demo有熱度。。。 但點開的一瞬間，你就是能感受到一種，模型永遠無法生成的東西—— 生命力。 那是很多程式設計師最初愛上寫程式碼時的模樣。 不是為了在求職流水線上刷穿幾百道LeetCode，不是為了在週報裡彙報又省了多少Token的呼叫賬單，更不是為了迎合大廠中層拍腦袋想出來的效能指標。 在這一切被功利化規訓之前，原本僅僅是在黑底白字的終端裡敲下幾行字元，看著螢幕上亮起的畫素點按照自己的心意運轉流動，就足以讓人興奮得通宵難眠。 我們親手造就了近乎無所不知的超級機器。 但卻似乎在不知不覺中，把人類最原始的探索欲與沉浸感，關在了門外…… title: 騰訊混元躋身最強開源模型！一手實測Hy4：搭配WorkBuddy，多模態Agent交付力拉滿
abstract: 騰訊混元躋身最強開源模型！一手實測Hy4：搭配WorkBuddy，多模態Agent交付力拉滿 聞樂 2026-11-09 16:44:00 來源： 量子位 聞樂 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號 QbitAI 混元Hy4正式交卷了！ 騰訊這次上來根本不跟你客氣，態度就明晃晃寫在臉上： 躋身最強開源模型之列 。 770B總參數、49B啟用參數， 首次引入原生視覺能力、首次支援電腦操作 。 指令遵循、長文理解和長程Agent能力也一起升級 ，電腦操作、長程Agent任務都擠進了開源陣營前排。 從preview到正式版，Hy4顯著擴展了預訓練和後訓練的資料與訓練規模，甚至還直接跑去跟一線業務搞起了“Co-Design”聯合打磨。 WorkBuddy國內版、國際版已經同步完成首發接入！ 我就先在WorkBuddy裡給它出了個難題：給我搓一把完全可互動的3D機械鍵盤出來。 75%配列、84鍵，鍵帽、軸體、定位板、PCB、電池和外殼，六層結構都安排上了。 滑鼠拽著能原地炸開看內部做工，裝回去還能直接上手敲，連按鍵下壓、彈簧受力回彈的物理動效都給你算進去了。 這麼一看，製作新品展示demo的活兒不就有人幹了？你說是吧Hy4～ Hy4已經在騰訊雲TokenHub、WorkBuddy/CodeBuddy、元寶、企業微信智慧助理大圓、ima等產品上線；API同步接入OpenRouter、Hermes、OpenCode等平臺。 QQ、王者榮耀、和平精英、微信讀書、騰訊新聞等騰訊系產品也在持續接入中。 模型權重也將於近期開源。 那咱也話不多說，先來實測一波。 畫素級視覺感知 Hy4首次引入的視覺理解，細節識別已經精細到 能夠在28億畫素航拍圖中，定位約2米的屋頂構件 。 這眼神兒是真不錯。 那咱接下來也考考它的眼力。 第一道題， 照著一張設計截圖，做一個復古風格的音樂播放器 。 先不說高畫質航拍圖，我就想看看，它到底能不能看懂排版細節。 Hy4接單之後先把圖裡的配色、字型、佈局挨個拆了一遍，連左側欄寬多少畫素都量好了，然後才開始寫程式碼，把頁面和播放功能一起搭起來。 中間裁切工具出了點偏差，它還換了個辦法，直接分析畫素來定位線條、提取顏色。 行，做題還自帶尺子和色卡。 看到成品的那一刻，我盯著螢幕看了足足半分鐘，不er，這還原度得99.9%吧—— 米色打底、橙紅點綴、黃綠配色，再加上粗粗的大標題和一張黑膠唱片，復古味兒一下就上來了。 導航、歌單、播放區域和待播列表，也都待在該待的位置。 我把買家秀和賣家秀並排放著找了半天不同，最顯眼的居然是左上角那倆前進後退按鈕：一個圓，一個方。。。 屬於是不拿放大鏡看，都不知道該從哪兒挑刺。 翻了翻Hy4的交付說明，播放暫停、上下首切換、拖動進度、調節音量都接上了，迴圈、隨機播放、搜尋和收藏同步也沒落下。 連手懶得碰滑鼠的情況都考慮到了：空格控制播放，方向鍵調整進度。 然而當我點下播放鍵才發現， 它連三首測試曲子都給備好了 。 我沒給它傳任何音訊檔案啊！ 影片地址：https://mp.weixin.qq.com/s/OThj_29CAuHn6ioaqjkSpQ 原來這些曲子是它用瀏覽器原生的Web Audio即時合成的，不用我再滿電腦翻音訊檔案，開啟網頁就能聽。 好好好，我只給了一張圖，Hy4不僅交付了播放器，還附贈測試曲庫，順手把試音的活兒也包了。 接著翻它的自測流水。 照記錄裡的過程，Hy4寫完程式碼後，自己悄悄在後臺拉起了一個無頭Chrome瀏覽器，在沙盒環境裡對著各個UI按鈕挨個點選、拖拽，一邊點一邊截圖做視覺差異對比。 第一輪其實也沒一把全過： 51項過了48項，兩項卡在測試指令碼，最後一項被它自己揪出來——列表放完最後一首歌，再點下一首時邏輯沒處理閉環。 它反手把這個邊緣Case改了，重新跑回歸。 最終報告顯示，59項測試全部通過，控制台報錯和執行時異常均為零。 光二維介面還不夠過癮，我又扔給Hy4一張遊樂場平面圖，讓它把園子給“立”起來。 設施在哪兒、多大，路怎麼拐彎，都得照著圖來；摩天輪和旋轉木馬也不能光站著擺造型，得轉起來；這遊樂園還得能讓我進去逛。 經歷了一連串幾何體建模、著色器配置和攝像機綁定，它真的把整座“星光遊樂園”原地拔地而起了。 經典的紅白旋轉木馬頂棚、主路兩旁的小賣部、沿街分佈的低多邊形樹木與草皮，全按比例投射進了三維空間。 低多邊形畫風也挺清爽，看著像個適合摸魚時進去溜達兩圈的小遊戲。 我本來都做好了進門先迷路的準備，右上角居然還配了張小地圖：設施、道路、草坪，連我現在站哪兒都標出來了。 進園後，WASD移動，滑鼠拖動轉向，按住Shift還能加速，想看設施就開啟標籤。 逛暈了還能一鍵返回入口，主打一個隨時找得著北。 它甚至準備了“沿道路自動巡遊”的按鈕，點一下，連路都不用自己走。 好嘛，讓它建個遊樂園，導覽服務也一起開張了。 影片地址：https://mp.weixin.qq.com/s/OThj_29CAuHn6ioaqjkSpQ Agent交付力拉滿 遊樂園逛完，回來乾點正事，試試Hy4這次重點強化的Agent和長程任務能力。 我給它塞了一份“拾光Beam Go 2”便攜智慧投影儀的產品資料，讓它做套15頁左右的新品介紹PPT。 Hy4先把資料從頭捋了一遍，配圖也沒瞎找，直接利用原生程式碼繪製風格高度統一的向量示意圖，圖表則保留成可編輯的形式，方便後續修改。 在渲染第4頁時，它發現一段長文本擠出了頁面安全邊框，自己在後臺立刻重構版式，把單欄拆成了卡片流，二次校驗通過後才繼續往下推進。 最後一共交了16頁PPT。行，還多送一頁。 不過，打工人都懂，PPT做完了，往往才是改PPT的開始。 我又扔給它一份完全不同視覺體系的暗黑高對比度模板，要求它按新版式重刷一遍。 Hy4倒沒急著把16頁全改了，先挑一頁試著套進去，確認沒問題，再批次修改剩下的頁面。 不得不說，邊驗證邊工作的能力是它這次非常亮眼的優勢，不是一股腦輸出完就交差，而是小步試錯、驗證通過再推進，大幅減少返工。 接著，我又給Hy4派了個活兒： 做一個高可用性的圖片批次處理工具。 裁切、改尺寸、壓縮、匯出，單張圖折騰幾下還行，一批圖挨個來，滑鼠沒壞，人先麻了。 這次乾脆把重複的手工操作交給它。 Hy4領到任務後，先在環境裡去研讀了業內開源標杆Squoosh和Image Workspace的優秀設計，借鑑了原圖/壓縮圖對比滑桿、預設工作流的技術方案。 然後快速拆分出上傳流、處理流、Web Worker多執行緒並行、Canvas圖形管線、ZIP歸檔模組，直接敲程式碼。 成品交付的時候，名字都起好了—— ATELIER影像批處理工作臺。 米白底色、橙色點綴，開啟先彈出三步引導。Slogan是：“把重複的交給工具，把審美留給自己。” 行，我負責審美，它負責重複。 按交付設計，圖片可以整批拖入，也能直接選資料夾；左側統一設定裁切、尺寸、壓縮和格式，少數需要“特殊照顧”的圖片，再單獨調整。 它還順手內建了社交頭像1:1、電商主圖、極小體積等常用配方，拉動滑桿能即時看畫質損失，最後點選一次打包成ZIP扔給瀏覽器下載。 影片地址：https://mp.weixin.qq.com/s/OThj_29CAuHn6ioaqjkSpQ 除此之外，Hy4現在還真能拿起滑鼠幹活。 開啟Chrome裡的JS Paint，用滑鼠臨摹混元親親表情包，還得把操作過程錄下來。 影片地址？：https://mp.weixin.qq.com/s/OThj_29CAuHn6ioaqjkSpQ 看螢幕、找工具、選顏色，再控制滑鼠落筆，用上的正是它新支援的CUA（計算機使用）能力。 好嘛，別的AI忙著一鍵出圖，Hy4在這兒練鼠繪，上有參考圖負責考眼力，下有畫圖軟體負責考手藝（doge）。 加量不加價 實測玩這麼一圈，我最大的感受是，Hy4在長程任務中的自主執行完成度高了很多。 面對多步驟任務，它能夠持續保持目標與任務狀態，在執行過程中進行階段性自檢，根據執行結果定位問題、修改方案，再重新驗證，直到能交付無Bug的結果。 我前面的案例確實也都是它自主執行、檢查和修改後的一次性交付結果。 Hy4的這輪訓練也更追求在真實生產力場景發揮作用。 前端最佳化細化到了複雜互動、業務邏輯、狀態管理及前後端聯動； 對Blender、CAD等專業軟體和跨應用長程任務也進行了專項訓練，強化任務規劃與執行能力。 辦公場景下，Hy4還圍繞時效檢索、多源資訊整合和事實一致性校驗，對搜尋鏈路進行了專項最佳化。 在內部測試中，Hy4的幻覺率由preview版的12.95%降至7.2%，推測類錯誤率由23.1%降至5.6%； 金融 這邊，Hy4還專門補了一輪專業課。 訓練覆蓋基金研究、證券分析、量化策略、資產配置、公司金融和財稅會計等方向，基於真實場景構建了數千個工作空間、上萬個高質量任務，讓模型學習專業流程與規範。 共有213位專家參與眾測，其中七成來自外部頭部金融機構，擁有五年以上工作經驗—— 這批閱卷人，可沒那麼好糊弄。 結果579個真實金融任務測下來，Hy4綜合表現位居開源模型第一。 看來這輪“進修”，還真沒白上。 科研 任務的跨度也正在擴大。 Hy4將複雜推理、科學程式設計與長程執行結合，在涵蓋7大學科、123項可執行研究任務的TenureTrail內部評測中，展現了數學構造、物理建模等領域的科研能力。 面對包含699萬個單細胞、整整84張沒有任何時間空間連續標記的二維無序小鼠胚胎切片的資料集還混雜著實驗切片中常見的映象翻轉等噪聲資料；在離線執行、無專用配準工具、無細胞型別標註的嚴苛條件下，Hy4耗時1.5小時，自主完成小鼠胚胎切片的空間對齊與三維網格重構。 全程零人工干預，最終對齊精細度甚至幹掉了專業配準工具的預設配置流程。 它也開始把複雜推理、科學程式設計和長程執行串起來。 在與北京大學數學團隊合作的研究中，Hy4找到了Méndez–Pinto–Villarreal猜想的反例，進一步提出新條件完善猜想，並對相關證明進行Lean形式化驗證。 這些能力現在已經可以通過WorkBuddy、CodeBuddy體驗。即日起至11月15日23:59還有 限時免費體驗 ！ 朋友們要是手上還有什麼擱了很久、總嫌麻煩的活兒，可以趁這會兒給Hy4安排一下~ 最後再提醒一波，主打極低推理成本、適合端側與高併發Agent編排的Hy4 flash也已經在路上了。 版權所有，未經授權不得以任何形式轉載及使用，違者必究。 混元 騰訊 聞樂 位元組找到了DeepSeek時強時弱的原因 2026-10-09 arXiv最嚴新規！每人每月最多提交2篇，拒稿不退額度 2026-10-02 DeepSeek擴招！彈性計算團隊大量HC，尤其需要資深工程師
