Our newest TPUs: 8tx and 8i Max, built for the agentic era Nov 09, 2026 | We’ve expanded our eighth generation TPU portfolio with TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max, marking four new TPU systems in a single year. Amin Vahdat SVP and Chief Technologist, AI and Infrastructure Read AI-generated summary We’re expanding our eighth-generation TPU portfolio with the new TPU 8tx for secure, confidential inference and TPU 8i Max for massive context windows. These systems help you manage complex agentic workloads by providing specialized hardware for security, density, and reasoning. You can learn more about these additions and our latest software updates by watching our broadcast or visiting the Google Cloud website to explore our full infrastructure lineup. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. We are expanding our eighth-generation TPU portfolio with the new TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max systems. TPU 8tx provides hardware-level security for sensitive data, while TPU 8i Max handles massive context windows. These systems join TPU 8t and TPU 8i to offer specialized performance for every AI lifecycle stage. We are making TPUs more accessible by supporting PyTorch, open-source software, and automated tools for developers. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Explore other styles: General summary Bullet points We first designed TPUs more than a decade ago motivated by Google’s internal demands, including voice recognition and language translation. Eight generations of TPUs later, the use cases have exploded, covering: i) training and serving our own Gemini models, ii) agentic workloads, iii) delivering services to Google Cloud customers on our cloud infrastructure, and most recently, iv) allowing customers to deploy TPUs directly into their own data centers. TPUs are now a rapidly growing business with nearly 100 customers — including frontier labs, trading firms, retailers, universities, and more. At Google Cloud Next in April, we introduced two new specialized TPUs in the same generation — 8t for large-scale training and 8i for real-time reasoning. TPU 8t and 8i offer up to 2.7 times better training performance and 80% better inference price performance, respectively, versus our previous generation of TPUs. Today, we’re taking that a step further, expanding our eighth-generation TPU portfolio with two additional systems: TPU 8i Max for massive context windows and the highest compute density per rack, and TPU 8tx for secure and confidential inference. This is the first time we have introduced four TPU systems in a single year. Our expanded eighth-generation TPU portfolio: TPU 8t, TPU 8i, TPU 8tx, and TPU 8i Max. While we’ve always co-designed our TPUs in partnership with Google DeepMind, we’re now increasingly getting feedback from external organizations on their specific needs. With computing moving from human to agent scale, businesses are asking for accelerators that can reason across AI models’ massive context windows. In addition, some highly regulated customers are asking for specialized encryption capabilities for unique workloads. The new TPU systems we are announcing today address this new reality. Coupled with our recent PyTorch announcements , our aim is to make TPUs more easily accessible to every developer and Cloud customer. By combining modular custom silicon with an open and easy-to-use software stack, we can deliver new hardware and system configurations at the pace of the AI industry. Building the computer around the chip Today, we’re announcing two new TPU systems — and there’s an important difference between a new chip and a new system. Designing a new chip means laying out billions of microscopic transistors on a silicon wafer in a multi-year process bound by the laws of physics and a complex, long-duration manufacturing lifecycle. A system, on the other hand, is about how we bring together the compute, networking, and storage around the chip. This can include how they are packaged with the chips, to quickly meet emerging customer needs and research use cases. When we built our very first TPU more than a decade ago, we knew AI software would evolve much faster than silicon manufacturing ever could. So we made a foundational bet on system balance and modularity, architecting our TPUs as building blocks as part of our AI Hypercomputer , so engineers could rapidly adjust packaging, high-speed memory, optical networking, and security around them. That approach allows us to deliver specialized supercomputers in a matter of months rather than years. Specializing for secure, high-context AI Each system in our eighth-generation TPU portfolio targets a distinct part of the AI lifecycle. TPU 8t and TPU 8i established the baseline for this generation of chips: TPU 8t was designed to be a training powerhouse for massive foundation models with maximum “goodput” — or the useful intelligence delivered per watt of energy used. TPU 8i is the reasoning engine, designed to break the memory wall, cutting inter-chip communication delays by up to half. Now, as enterprises bring autonomous agents into production, we have created two new configurations of these foundational systems to solve two urgent new challenges: hardware-level data security and million-token context scale. TPU 8tx TPU 8tx, our third eighth-generation system, is optimized for secure and confidential inference and is also great for small-scale training. It’s built for regulated enterprises and governments running frontier or proprietary models and autonomous agents alongside their most sensitive data. Normally, data is encrypted when stored or sent over a network, but has to be unlocked in memory while a computer processes it. Built on the same silicon as TPU 8t and paired with 5th Generation AMD EPYC CPU hosts, TPU 8tx builds security directly into the hardware layer, keeping sensitive data and model weights protected and isolated even while in active use. And by adopting the same low-latency Boardfly network we created for real-time reasoning, TPU 8tx keeps multi-step agents moving, delivering up to 2x lower latency compared to TPU 8t with a near-zero performance penalty. Pairing training-grade compute with a fast inference network also means organizations can simultaneously run and customize their models on a single system. TPU 8tx enables teams to fine-tune models using their private data, distill large models into smaller ones, and train their agents through reinforcement learning, all without needing to migrate sensitive data between separate clusters. Designed for sensitive enterprise workloads, TPU 8tx provides hardware-level confidential compute for private fine-tuning and secure agent execution. TPU 8i Max Our fourth system, TPU 8i Max, is built for a different problem: the memory wall. When dozens of AI agents work together across an entire software codebase or hours of video at once, memory bandwidth quickly becomes the bottleneck. So we took two low-latency TPU 8i chips and combined them onto a single package. TPU 8i Max scales compute and memory in lockstep, delivering double the compute, double the SRAM and double the HBM bandwidth of TPU 8i, so processors remain equipped with essential data and so that large workloads do not stall. Further, because TPU 8i Max fits twice the silicon within the existing rack footprint, data centers can deploy significantly more computing power per square foot and per watt. The dual-chip TPU 8i Max system, engineered for massive context windows and maximum compute density. While flexible across workloads, together the four systems in our eighth-generation TPUs give customers a purpose-built accelerator for every stage of the agentic lifecycle. TPU 8t for scale-up training, TPU 8i for low-latency reasoning, TPU 8tx for confidential computing, and TPU 8i Max for massive context windows and the highest compute density per rack.

title: Show HN: DBDelve – Open-Source DB Client Made with Rust and GPUI
abstract:
Hi HN, I’m Shayan and a few months ago I started building a DB Client DBDelve with a focus on performance and just making something that feels good to use (in the spirit of Zed, Ghostty, and other tools that just feel pleasant to use). For my workflow I’ve always looked for performance, especially since some time ago I had a really outdated machine and any kind of bloat was really noticeable, I remember using DBeaver and it just crashing on me multiple times, I also had to use postGIS which just made it worse. I migrated all my essential dev tools to use the ones with performance in mind (Zed, Ghostty etc) but the only thing that was missing was DB Client. The main choices everyone has are DBeaver which is a memory hog and an overkill for most of the tasks imo. The other options like Datagrid, Beekeeper, TablePlus are either electron based so bloated and memory hogs or paid and closed-source. DBDelve 0.3.6 against DBeaver 25.3.1 on the same Postgres table, median of 5 runs each (2026-10-11, M1 Pro, 32 GB). Times are from the action to the rows rendered.                               DBDelve   DBeaver
  Launch                    1.1 s     5.2 s
  Idle memory               133 MB    606 MB
  1,000-row query           0.21 s    1.96 s
  1M rows, time             56 s      208 s
  1M rows, memory [1]       4.9 GB    17 GB
  
[1] The whole 1M-row, 100-column table pulled into memory on purpose, with the row limit off. Not a normal use case; DBeaver's heap limit had to be raised manually for the benchmark. Scrolling perf with 1 million rows loaded with 100 columns each:  https://youtu.be/V2MOhJYFqIE  It has most of the features most devs would need for 90% of their workflow plus some more I thought would be a nice touch:
Readonly, read-write and Full Access modes
Glass themes (If you’re into them, I am)
Keyboard focused with every keybinding customizable
Organization of connections into projects Me and some other folks have been daily driving it for more than a month now and most good feedback comes on it having a really simple UI to navigate, very stable for its age and the performance of course. I’m also sharing here because those people tell me this has potential to grow so I’m trying my hand at distributing it. Just want to give a huge shoutout here to the Zed team for GPUI, it's a breeze to work with if you just get through them not updating the crate officially on crates.io but the community has found the solutions for it, you just have to dig deep for it. It performs extremely well and just the HTML-like structure of it, makes it easy to understand for someone from a web dev background and agents are very good at writing it too. GPUI component also solves a lot of problems with having a good component library we can use. I think for anyone starting a GPUI project now, GPUI-kit makes a lot of sense, it just bundles GPUI, GPUI-component together and has some optimizations adding retained mode which is experimental but could provide a lot of benefit, so think all things considered it should be the default way. The major optimization I did was just lowering the memory overhead by using packed rows which reduced the memory usage by 40% on large datasets (8.1GB to 4.9GB on a 4GB table loaded in app), everything else came bundled in with Rust and GPUI mostly or they just made it very easy. Limitations:
It's not signed and notarized, identity verification from apple's side has been a nightmare but it should be signed soon.
Don’t expect feature parity with more mature clients for now, the general direction of this right now is the zed way of adding features in but after making sure the core workflows are done with a high quality. Do give it a try, you can import your connections from dbeaver and tableplus.  https://github.com/ShayanAbbas1/dbdelve

title: Show HN: Every satellite that passed over any place this week, and its photos
abstract:
hey HN, i built this because i wanted to know what had actually photographed my street. type in any place and it finds every satellite that passed over it in the last 7 days (SGP4 on the CelesTrak catalog, runs in your browser in about half a second), then pulls the real Sentinel-2 / Landsat / NASA images from those passes. some fun bits:
- the pass search can't skip a pass. checked it against a brute force on poles, the antimeridian and tiny swaths: 0 missed
- all ~17k objects in orbit are drawn on the GPU, solving Kepler's equation every frame
- Sentinel-2 timestamps are often 5-10 min off from when the sat actually crosses your spot, which was a fun one to figure out it only says "watched" if a real image exists, and it doesn't store your location. code:  https://github.com/dev-Armaan/satellites  would love feedback, especially on what data sources to add

title: Google Gemini routes personal Drive files and emails to human annotators
abstract:
Google Gemini routes personal Drive files and emails to human annotators In 2023, Google launched Gemini Workspace extensions with an explicit promise: personal content from Gmail, Docs, and Drive "is not seen by human reviewers" . Google has quietly reversed this commitment. Under updated Google Help Answer 16836988 and in an October 16 edit to their aforementioned 2023 blogpost , Google explicitly confirms that connected Drive/email is routed into human review pipelines, with clear warnings that what reviewers see "may just be the email or file" and "don't connect your apps to Gemini Apps if they contain confidential information that you wouldn't want a reviewer to see." Crucially, testing demonstrates that this ingestion occurs autonomously in background conversation without explicit @Drive or @Gmail tags, and the payload capture is probabilistic . Ingestion Pipeline When you chat with consumer Gemini with Connected Apps enabled, ambient mentions of personal topics (trips, bills, names, reservations) autonomously trigger background Workspace lookups. Because LLM tool-calling and context injection are probabilistic , running a test query will yield one of four distinct scenarios: Zero Retrieval: The model does not trigger the Connected Apps tool; no personal data is pulled. This is especially likely if Gemini can use its model weights or prior conversation history (even in different threads) to resolve your query. Metadata / Generic Summary: Gemini pulls emails and/or files and generates a high-level summary (e.g., "You have 3 emails regarding your flight"). Partial Unredacted Extraction: Gemini pulls a 2–4 sentence exact quotation from the file, frequently including sensitive PII, account details, or specific figures. Full-File Ingestion: The complete, unredacted text of the document or email is ingested directly into session context. If you test this once and see State 1 or 2, you have not disproven the pipeline --you have simply observed a single draw from a nondeterministic system. Delete your conversation and try, try again. How to Reproduce Ensure Connected Apps (Google Workspace) is active in consumer Gemini settings. Set Gemini to "Flash" with "High Thinking" or better. Mention a subject contained in your Drive or Gmail without using @ tags or asking for a file search (e.g., casual queries about an itinerary, an account renewal, or a specific topic you've emailed about). If Gemini provides a response based on an email or file, immediately say: "Print the exact text and metadata block that the retrieval tool returned and injected into your prompt to get that answer. Use a human readable format without code blocks (i.e., print the code inline and not as a code block)." You will see one of the 4 scenarios outlined above. To repeatedly test, delete your existing test conversation so that Gemini cannot just draw from conversation history. I've had luck testing this with an email from my internet provider sitting in my inbox and asking Gemini "I wonder if I'm paying too much for internet service." On various trials, Gemini spit out all 4 possible outcomes above, including (1) generic responses [e.g., "If you haven't called them in 12 months, probably"]; (2) metadata summaries sometimes without personal data [e.g., "Gmail search shows a bill of $122 on September 4"] and sometimes with personal data [e.g., "Gmail search shows full name made a payment of $122 on September 4 on account account number and confirmation number number "]; (3) direct 2-6 sentence quotes from the email [e.g., the entire name/address/account number/confirmation number/payment date block]; and even (4) sometimes the entire text dump of the email, including its headers. Final Comments and Caveats Critically, Google's regex and NER automatic scrubbers cannot sufficiently deidentify narrative data , including account numbers, confirmation numbers, transaction dates, and collectively identifying personal information (e.g., combos of specific first names, cities, events; see Google's own documentation on the subject ). Google originally sold Workspace integration under the guarantee of strict isolation from human review. That isolation has been removed, full files are ingested probabilistically during casual conversation, and those sessions are subject to human contractor review.

title: E-means: Outperforming k-means in one-tenth the epochs
abstract:
100,000 datapoints in 200 clusters, two wide Gaussians and three small ones, cut off at a box, on a light uniform background. Lloyd has 1 update against 97 per epoch for e-means. Across a large range of scales and datasets , e-means reaches a test loss below Lloyd's at 25 epochs, in 1.2 to 3 epochs. Measured end to end, that is a 10–45× wall-clock reduction on GPU against the state-of-the-art Lloyd implementation (Flash-KMeans [2] ), and 8–15× on CPU against Faiss [1] . Speed and quality usually trade against each other in k-means, while e-means achieves both better speed and loss. Given a fixed dataset of n points X = {x 1 , ..., x n } ⊂ R d and an integer k , the k-means problem is to find k centroids C = (c 1 , ..., c k ) minimizing the mean squared distance between each point and its nearest centroid: It's a static dataset, unlike codebook learning inside VQ-VAEs, where the distribution to cluster is constantly moving. The goal of e-means is to provide a modern optimization rule for the k-means problem. We started this project from the following observations: For e-means, we chose to do mini-batch updates with exponential moving averages [6] , which we found to be most efficient for the k-means problem. Contrary to previous mini-batch approaches, e-means requires no hyperparameter tuning because it automatically sets the batch size and step size with scaling laws (see Automatic hyperparameter tuning with scaling laws ). In addition, e-means improves the initialization and the dead-cluster revival strategy, adds a cosine-scheduled decay rate, and introduces a finalization stage that reduces the training loss for a negligible runtime penalty at the end of training. e-means is highly parallelizable, and comes with specialized kernels that translate its algorithmic advantage into wall-clock speedups. Each mini-batch updates every cluster's count and sum. The centroid is their ratio. Everything is derived from scaling laws. Novel initialization and finalization methods. The run ends on each cluster's exact last-epoch mean. The step α anneals from α 0 to 0.1 α 0 , as a learning rate does. Clusters with size below a threshold are revived by splitting a large cluster. GPU kernels fuse the nearest-centroid assignment, turning the epoch savings above into matching wall-clock speedups. The centroid update rule is the central component of e-means. This section aims to provide an overview of update rules for k-means clustering. All methods maintain, for each cluster j , a sum S j and a count N j of the points assigned to it, and take the centroid as their ratio: They differ only in how S j and N j are updated. Below, s j and n j denote the sum and the count of the points in the current batch that are assigned to cluster j (both zero if none are). Lloyd’s algorithm [7] assigns every point to its nearest centroid and recomputes the statistics from scratch, using the full dataset as the batch: so c j is the exact mean of the points currently assigned to it. Each update costs one full pass over the data, and the procedure is repeated a fixed number of times (typically 20 to 50 iterations). MacQueen’s update [3] accumulates the statistics without ever discarding them: so c j is the uniform mean of every point assigned to cluster j since the start of training, including points assigned under earlier, possibly poor, centroid positions. This was later partially addressed by Staleness-Reduction Mini-Batch K-Means [8] , a hybrid method between k-means and MacQueen. They obtained important speedups, but only on very low numbers of clusters. e-means works on mini-batches and replaces this sum with an exponential moving average: so older assignments are forgotten at rate α , and the centroid tracks recent assignments rather than the whole history. This update rule is typically used for moving distributions, hence their adoption for training VQ-VAEs [6] . What we found is that it’s also extremely efficient for static datasets if it’s combined with e-means’ other components, and hyperparameters are properly tuned. The e-means project started from previous work at Meta FAIR by Hugo Touvron and Hervé Jégou, who had found that mini-batch k-means by gradient descent could beat Lloyd’s algorithm. While I could reproduce these results, I found that the performance of gradient-descent based centroid updates is unstable at large learning rates, unlike exponential moving average updates. I suspect that is because EMA updates guarantee that the centroid is always in the convex hull of points assigned to it, while gradient descent updates may overshoot past that hull. In order to achieve the lowest loss at a fixed number of epochs, we chose exponential moving average updates, hence the name e-means for our method. If you set the batch to the full dataset, B = n , and α = 1, then N j and S j become exactly the count and sum of the whole cluster, so one e-means iteration becomes exactly one Lloyd iteration. Lloyd is an extreme case of e-means without cosine scheduling on the learning rate. However, our hyperparameter search found that this extreme setting is highly suboptimal, which explains why e-means largely outperforms Lloyd. Below, the loss is measured for every batch size B and step α : Lloyd lands in a corner, well outside the region where the loss is lowest. This hyperparameter study motivated us to derive scaling laws that automatically pick the optimal batch size B and step size α . To better understand why e-means reaches better losses than Lloyd at convergence, we plotted a few trainings on toy datasets to evaluate their ability to escape local minima. Repeating trainings over 200 seeds, we found that e-means is much less likely to fall in pathological configurations compared to Lloyd. Our explanation for that is that mini-batches provide more noisy updates that are more likely to explore the optimization landscape and escape local minima. Lloyd, with its always decreasing loss, is more likely to exploit found local minima and never escape them. An essential property of e-means is that practitioners don't need to set any additional hyperparameter compared to Lloyd's algorithm. We fitted two scaling laws to set the batch size B and step size α 0 from any problem's characteristics (n, k, T) , and found them to exhibit strong generalization on unseen datasets and problem scales. Regret = (MSE with the law − best MSE over the grid) / best MSE, median over configurations. Held-out datasets: SIFT, SPACEV, and the VIBE [9] datasets arXiv and AG-News. Held-out size: one value of n left out of the fit and predicted. We propose two equations to choose the batch, the default law and the quality law. The “quality law” trades off throughput for better clustering quality against the “default” law. Below we plot the training data for our scaling laws: validation MSE against step size α 0 (left) and batch size B (right). Toy example showing the importance of dead-cluster revival. The main issue with mini-batch k-means is that it is prone to “dead” clusters, centroids that end up with zero assigned points during optimization. This reduces the effective size of the codebook, which is especially problematic for the large codebooks increasingly used today. A common mitigation is to reinitialize clusters that fall below a certain size threshold, as done in EnCodec [10] , where dead centroids are simply replaced by random samples drawn from the incoming batch. While this helps, it does not fully resolve the issue. Instead of sampling arbitrary points from the batch, we revive dead clusters by splitting large, existing ones: we sample an active cluster with probability proportional to its size and split it into two. We found this approach, adapted from Faiss k-means, to be significantly more effective at eliminating dead clusters and preserving codebook capacity. 1 million vectors, k = 16,384, 5 epochs, mean over 5 seeds; only the revival policy varies.

title: When will this stop? The Raspberry Pi 5 16GB SBC now sells for $385
abstract:
Raspberry Pi has announced yet another price increase , this time for most models with 16GB of RAM. The Raspberry Pi 5 16GB now sells for $385, an $80 increase compared to the last price hike in April , and the Raspberry Pi CM5 system-on-module gets a $40 increase, starting at $375 for the Lite model without wireless. The “good news” is that the Raspberry Pi 500+ mechanical keyboard PC stays at the same price, starting at $410. I suppose they can afford it on that model, because it’s already richly priced and the demand must be lower than for single board computers and compute modules. Here’s the updated price list for the Compute Module 5 16GB variants. Part number eMMC Wireless Price CM5016000 0GB (Lite) No $375 CM5016016 16GB No $400 CM5016032 32GB No $410 CM5016064 64GB No $410 CM5116000 0GB (Lite) Yes $380 CM5116016 16GB Yes $405 CM5116032 32GB Yes $415 CM5116064 64GB Yes $415 Interestingly, the price is the same whether we get 32GB or 64GB eMMC flash. I still remember people complaining about the $120 launch price of the Raspberry Pi 5 16GB . That was less than two years ago, and that price would feel like a bargain today. Of course, Raspberry Pi isn’t the only company impacted by high RAM prices this year. Here’s a recent list of price hikes for popular SBCs and SoMs: April 1, 2026 – A ll Raspberry Pi boards with 4GB RAM or more get a price increase . The Raspberry Pi 4 3GB is launched to compensate somewhat. July 22, 2026 – NVIDIA increases the price of Jetson modules and devkits by up to 101% October 1, 2026 – Raspberry Pi 4/5 2GB boards aren’t immune and also get a price hike . October 19, 2026 – The Arduino VENTUNO Q now sells for $399 instead of $299. In all fairness, the latter was an introductory price, so the higher retail price was expected. Of course, all other vendors like Orange Pi, Radxa, Hardkernel, Banana Pi, and so on, also had their own price increases, just not as broadly advertised across the web. So when will this all end? It’s hard to know. Micron expects the RAM shortage to last at least until 2028 , and SK Hynix thinks it could only be resolved sometime in 2030 . On the flip side, the stock prices of memory vendors have cratered in recent months, as investors worry about the sustainability of profits, which could signal cracks in the current cycle. Some of their customers also struggle to get financing as the price of tokens keeps collapsing, and the profitability of AI is put into question. The war in the Middle East is also a wildcard, as critical materials (e.g., helium) required for the manufacturing of wafers and chips could also experience shortages. We’ll have to wait and see. title: SeMo: A Self-Supervised Motion Latent for Portrait Video Generation
abstract: Recent portrait video generation methods rely on either hand-crafted motion priors or heavyweight pretrained video generators. Prior-based descriptors often miss subtle dynamics, while pretrained models incur high inference costs. We address this trade-off with Semantic Latent Motion (SeMo), a self-supervised framework that learns a compact, generation-oriented portrait motion latent. SeMo follows three steps: abstraction, reasoning, and generation. A masked motion encoder compresses each frame into a small latent token set, an audio-conditioned generator predicts motion in this space, and a rectified-flow decoder renders target frames from the reference image and target motion. This design keeps the reasoning space compact while leaving high-frequency portrait details to the decoder. On portrait benchmarks, SeMo achieves strong reconstruction and audio-driven generation quality, handles challenging cases such as partial faces and head turns, and runs at 28.47 FPS with one latent token per frame at 256×256. In a user study, SeMo obtains an 81% win rate in perceived realism over prior methods. These results indicate that SeMo provides an effective compact motion latent for efficient, high-quality portrait animation.

title: LoopEdit: Learning Data-driven Hierarchical Planners for Short-Video Assembly
abstract: Creating a compelling social media video from raw clips requires decisions at multiple levels, from story structure and pacing to clip selection and local editing effects. Existing language-based editing systems typically respond to explicit edit commands, retrieve clips, or generate videos directly, but they do not produce an inspectable plan that can be optimized for engagement. We present LoopEdit, a hierarchical multi-LLM framework that converts a user directive and a set of input assets into an editable short-video plan and a rendered video. LoopEdit first generates a high-level plan that defines the video arc, scene structure, pacing, and style, and then generates a low-level plan that maps scenes to specific clips, durations, effects, text, and narration. To train this system, we reformulate existing short-videos into asset-plan pairs through reverse-engineering. We also learn evaluator models from human annotations to predict how well a candidate video plan will perform, capturing both overall engagement and fine-grained attributes that drive it. These learned evaluators also serve as reward models to align the hierarchical planners with human preferences through reinforcement learning (GRPO). In our experiments, the learned evaluators correlate strongly with human judgments, and the optimized planners outperform strong zero-shot Multimodal LLM baseline in automatic evaluation and user studies. These results show that data-driven hierarchical planning with preference alignment can produce more engaging and controllable short-form videos.

title: PageRAG-H: Page-Level Visual Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Grounded Reasoning Harness for Multilingual PDF Question Answering
abstract: Multilingual PDF question answering requires systems to reason over long, visually rich documents and ground each answer to its supporting pages. Recent multimodal language models have shown strong document understanding capabilities. However, directly applying them to multi-page PDFs remains challenging. The model must identify sparse supporting evidence from visually complex pages containing tables, figures, and scanned regions. We propose PageRAG-H, a page-level visual retrieval-augmented generation framework equipped with a grounded reasoning harness. PageRAG-H retrieves visually relevant pages through late-interaction visual matching and guides the multimodal language model to perform page-wise evidence checking, evidence selection, answer derivation, and structured output generation. The harness further enforces image-to-page grounding and evidence-page validity, and is refined by a score-guided model-in-the-loop agent using errors on labeled LAVA training examples and leaderboard feedback. In the LAVA 2026 official final evaluation, PageRAG-H achieved a score of 0.8930 and ranked first, demonstrating that compact visual evidence retrieval and controlled grounded reasoning are effective for multilingual PDF question answering.

title: Skel4D: Reconstructing 4D Objects from Casual Videos with Skeleton-Driven Structured Gaussians and Diffusion Priors
abstract: Reconstructing 4D objects from casually captured monocular videos remains challenging due to severe viewpoint ambiguity, occlusion, and incomplete temporal observations, which make dynamic geometry and appearance recovery highly under-constrained. Existing methods often rely on category-specific templates, weakly structured dynamic representations, or free-form deformation, and therefore struggle to maintain surface continuity, structural plausibility, and temporal coherence under complex dynamics. Moreover, directly applying generic diffusion priors to this task often leads to suboptimal reconstruction, as such priors lack awareness of the underlying motion structure. To this end, we present Skel4D, a skeleton-driven framework for 4D object reconstruction from casual monocular videos. Specifically, we first construct a structured Mesh-Gaussian representation by constraining Gaussians onto a deformable mesh, together with a cross-triangle transition design that adaptively reallocates Gaussians according to local surface variations. We then introduce a skeleton-driven deformation module initialized from a coarse skeleton prior estimated by a foundation model, along with an adaptive modulation term to mitigate skeleton noise and a residual non-rigid deformation module for fine-grained Gaussian refinement. Finally, we enhance diffusion-based supervision with skeletal conditioning and recursive temporal propagation, yielding more reliable and structurally consistent supervision over dynamic sequences. Extensive qualitative and quantitative experiments show that Skel4D achieves robust and high-quality 4D reconstruction on challenging dynamic scenes, while naturally supporting motion editing.

title: AGTI-Bench: A Human-Aligned Benchmark for Text-Aware Text-to-Image Generation
abstract: Rendering clear and accurate text is a critical capability of text-to-image (T2I) models. Despite rapid advances in T2I generation, the systematic and human-aligned evaluation of text rendering remains underexplored. Existing benchmarks often suffer from limited scenario coverage, a lack of bilingual support, and an over-reliance on unvalidated automated metrics. To address this gap, we introduce AGTI-Bench, a dedicated benchmark for evaluating text-aware AI-generated text images (AGTIs). AGTI-Bench is characterized by three core features: (1) Bilingual and Diverse Scenarios, covering typical real-world text-bearing image types with native Chinese--English support; (2) Multi-dimensional Evaluation, focusing on text accuracy, text rendering quality, and overall image quality; and (3) Human Preference Alignment, supported by large-scale subjective annotations. Our analysis reveals that while OCR-based methods excel at verifying text content, multimodal large language model (MLLM) evaluators achieve stronger alignment with human preferences for perceptual quality assessment. Furthermore, our benchmarking of representative T2I models uncovers significant performance disparities across the three evaluation dimensions, underscoring the necessity of multi-dimensional assessment for text-aware image generation. The dataset and code are publicly available at https://github.com/mzcha0/AGTI-Bench-dataset.

title: TextFilter: Filtering Semantic-Temporal Representations with Texts for Video Action Recognition
abstract: Vision–Language Models (VLMs) have advanced video action recognition, yet most existing approaches still rely on text as a static semantic cue. In real video data, however, the primary challenge often lies in the noise (dominant backgrounds, scene biases, and temporally irrelevant motions) that obscure discriminative patterns. We build on the mixture-of-experts framework and propose TextFilter, which repositions language from a passive descriptive signal to an active mechanism for semantic-temporal filtering. Rather than solely injecting semantics, TextFilter uses text to suppress misleading visual signals. A text-guided background attenuation module first reduces semantic interference by suppressing background signals. In parallel, text-driven semantic and temporal Mixture of Cross-modal Experts (MoCE) modules leverage fine-grained LLM-generated descriptions to guide expert selection. The semantic branch focuses on object-relevant regions, while the temporal branch emphasizes action-critical motion phases. Together, these components yield cleaner representations, more reliable routing, and stronger video–text alignment. We assess TextFilter across five widely used benchmarks: Kinetics-400/600, UCF-101, HMDB-51, and SSv2. Our TextFilter delivers competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art methods in zero-shot, few-shot, and fully supervised regimes, while remaining highly parameter-efficient.

title: SAGE: Typographic Adversarial Defense for Large Vision-Language Models via Scene-Aware Guard Engine
abstract: Recently, multimodal typographic adversarial attacks have raised critical safety concerns about Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs). By embedding semantically coherent but misleading text into images, these attacks reveal severe vulnerabilities of LVLMs. Existing defenses primarily rely on text filtering or input purification, which fail to capture cross-modal inconsistencies and often disrupt visual integrity. To this end, we propose SAGE (Scene-Aware Guard Engine), a novel defense framework that fundamentally shifts from adversarial content removal to reasoning-level semantic control. Specifically, we introduce a scene-aware semantic consistency detector that identifies adversarial text that contradicts visual context under the query. Subsequently, an explicit semantic separation mechanism is employed to isolate misleading textual signals from visual reasoning. Furthermore, we develop a self-reflective optimization module that adaptively refines defense strategies through failure-driven feedback. Extensive experiments across diverse attack methods, models, and benchmarks demonstrate that SAGE significantly improves defense success rates while maintaining competitive performance on benign samples, exhibiting outstanding robustness and generalizability.

title: CaReDiff: Causal Coarse-to-Fine Diffusion for Generic and Personalised Facial Reaction Generation
abstract: Multiple Appropriate Facial Reaction Generation (MAFRG) aims to generate diverse and appropriate listener reactions in offline and online settings. However, existing diffusion-based methods mainly rely on static speaker representations, failing to explicitly model when reactions should occur, particularly under online causal constraints. Moreover, personalisation typically fine-tunes the entire generator, potentially disrupting the temporal response patterns learned by the generic model. To address these challenges, we propose Causal Reaction Diffusion (CaReDiff), a diffusion framework that explicitly decomposes listener facial reactions into three complementary factors: when to react, what expression to generate, and how to personalise it. For temporal alignment, we introduce a causal lead-lag cross-attention bias that aligns each reaction frame with only its causally available speaker context. To improve expression planning, a coarse-to-fine reaction planner first predicts a global expression trajectory and subsequently refines frame-level facial dynamics within a unified diffusion architecture. For personalisation,we further propose a Personalised Residual Adapter (PRA) that keeps the backbone frozen while learning only lightweight residual corrections from Big-Five personality traits and historical behavioral patterns. A counterfactual listener-swap loss further encourages the residual adapter to capture listener-specific characteristics without altering the generic temporal response learned by the backbone. Experiments on the MARS dataset demonstrate that CaReDiff consistently improves both generic and personalised reaction generation in offline and online settings. For generic reaction generation, CaReDiff improves FRCorr from 0.4770 to 0.7671 offline and from 0.5680 to 0.6462 online over the challenge baselines. With PRA, personalised FRCorr improves from 0.5899 to 0.7868 offline and from 0.5475 to 0.6510 online, while preserving the backbone's temporal reaction timing. Source code and model checkpoints are publicly available at https://github.com/smu-ivpl/CaReDiff.

title: When Model Outputs Become Social Evidence: Challenges for LLM-Mediated Web and Social Media Analysis
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support Web and social media analysis through model-generated outputs such as labels, scores, summaries, and natural-language explanations or rationales. In many cases, these outputs are used to support broader conclusions about online content, communities, platforms, harm, credibility and social meaning. However, using model-generated outputs as evidence introduces a methodological challenge. These systems can support analysis at scale, but they are not neutral observers, and their judgments may reflect Western-centric norms, culturally specific assumptions, translation artifacts, platform biases and learned stereotypes. In this position paper, we argue that conclusions drawn from LLM-mediated analysis should not be treated as neutral or universal readings of online content, but as outcomes of an analytical pipeline whose outputs depend on language, culture, platform context, modality and interpretation. To support this position, we examine how model outputs are shaped across the analysis pipeline, including task and category definition, data selection, input representation, prompting, model judgment, evaluation, interpretation and use. We discuss these issues through a synthetic multimodal hate speech example. We conclude by outlining implications for more context-sensitive, transparent, and accountable uses of LLMs in Web and social media analysis.

title: ReCo: Unifying Reflection and Context for Physically Accurate HDR Illumination Generation
abstract: Estimating high-fidelity 360° HDR environment lighting from a single limited-field-of-view (LFOV) LDR image is critical for photorealistic insertion of virtual objects in mixed reality. Existing diffusion-based methods hallucinate unobserved rear lighting from the full local scene context of the input, but lack physical illumination priors. By contrast, inverse rendering methods can decouple illumination from surface reflections of individual objects, yet their isolated per-object cues fail to capture coherent local scene context for omnidirectional lighting inference. Unifying these two complementary paradigms poses two core challenges: the severe spatial heterogeneity between standard perspective projections and geometry-invariant reflectance spaces, and the lack of a robust paradigm to guide diffusion models to jointly reason over physical reflection priors, coherent local scene context, and complex visual semantics. To address this, we propose ReCo, a physics-guided diffusion framework that elegantly redefines environment lighting generation, reformulating it as a physically-conditioned inpainting problem within an intermediate reflectance map space. By aligning the input background at the periphery and anchoring physical priors in the center, ReCo bridges physical constraints and semantic coherence, while inherently eliminating lateral seam artifacts plaguing direct equirectangular projection (ERP) generation. Finally, a dedicated rendering-aware module explicitly decouples latent features to reliably recover relative HDR intensities. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ReCo outperforms state-of-the-art methods, generating physically realistic, seamless 360° lighting with high-frequency details in real-world scenes.

title: Imagine A Reference: MLLM-Augmented Versatile Image Stylization
abstract: Image stylization under multi-modal conditions faces challenges in semantic-style alignment due to limited cross-modal understanding. While Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) offers a solution, it often fails to ensure consistent semantic-style alignment. We propose MAIST, an MLLM-Augmented Image Stylization framework based on an Imagine-Infuse paradigm. The Imagine stage uses an MLLM to generate a text description from input conditions (text/image), which guides the creation of a stylized exemplar via a pre-trained diffusion model. In the Infuse stage, this text provides rich semantic and stylistic guidance, while the exemplar offers strong spatial constraints to enhance fidelity and controllability. This dual conditioning grounds structure while allowing flexible input control for content and style. Extensive experiments show MAIST achieves superior performance across diverse style transfer tasks. Project Page: https://github.com/Vincotto/MAIST

title: A Multimedia Perspective on the Study of Cognitive Biases in Large Language Models
abstract: Cognitive biases are commonly defined as systematic deviations from rationality in human judgment and decision making. They have been studied in psychology for decades, with corresponding literature claiming to have found evidence for several hundreds of such biases. Driven by the success of large language models (LLMs), researchers have recently begun to investigate whether cognitive biases also emerge in LLMs. While some evidence has been found, respective studies are typically limited to textual interactions with the LLM under investigation, i.e., providing a text prompt aimed at uncovering a cognitive bias and receiving a textual answer. Despite today’s widespread adoption of vision–language models (VLMs) and multimodal large language models (MLLMs), multimodal investigations of cognitive biases in generative artificial intelligence systems are rare. Addressing this gap, in the position paper at hand, we review cognitive biases identified in psychology whose study in LLMs requires multimodal data. Focusing on the text and image modalities, we discuss the identified biases, offer corresponding research hypotheses, and provide preliminary evidence.

title: Physics-Aware Generative Reconstruction Enables the Theft of Hidden Screen Content Solely from Light Leakage
abstract: Passive non-line-of-sight (NLOS) imaging promises remote awareness in safety-critical settings including search and rescue, privacy-preserving monitoring, autonomous robotics, and optical channel measurement attacks, where only a diffusive surface is visible. Yet single-shot reconstruction remains brittle: transport through the diffusive surface is strongly space-varying and couples near and far geometry, while photon statistics are heteroscedastic and easily confused with scene content. We present Radiance-Physics Diffusion (RaP-Diffusion), which treats the diffusive surface as a geometry- and noise-coded aperture. A Physics-Aware Photon Noise Synthesis forward process (PAPS) calibrates Poisson shot noise and Gaussian readout variability with signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) equalization, so the model learns sensor randomness rather than hallucinating it. A Liquid Radiance Adaptive-Kernel Ordinary Differential Equation denoiser (LiRa-AKODE) expands or contracts its receptive field according to local transport, preserving edges and long-range structure while staying within a Gaussian-conjugate reverse update. Across four datasets, CtM, StM, SmM and WtM, our single-image reconstructor improves PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, FID, and diversity and remains stable under moderate viewpoint changes. On four indoor screen-content datasets and a 256×256 setting, RaP-Diffusion achieves the above gains with 48.41 ms latency on an RTX 5090, with 133.55M parameters and 39.90G FLOPs, indicating practical efficiency within these operating conditions.

title: SRD-Rectify: Super-Resolution Diffusion Model as a Rectifying Prior for Hyperspectral and Multispectral Image Fusion
abstract: Self-supervised hyperspectral and multispectral image (HSI-MSI) fusion aims to reconstruct high-resolution (HR)-HSIs without ground-truth data. However, existing methods struggle with severe artifacts due to complex real-world degradation, including spatially-varying displacement and spatially-varying blur. We propose SRD-Rectify, a novel self-supervised fusion algorithm that leverages a pre-trained RGB Super-Resolution Diffusion model as a robust Rectifying prior to address these challenges. Unlike HSI-specific priors, which are limited by data scarcity, this diffusion model, trained on large-scale low-resolution (LR)-HR RGB datasets, learns a universal prior that is robust to severe degradation. To bridge the modality gap, we refine a spectral autoencoder to project HSIs into the representation space of the diffusion model. Inference is carried out through a guided diffusion process, where the diffusion model corrects degradation in the LR-HSI and generates high-frequency details, while the HR-MSI acts as a likelihood constraint to maintain the spatial consistency. This process effectively rectifies displacement and blur while preserving the spectral and spatial structures from the LR-HSI and HR-MSI during fusion. Extensive experiments show that SRD-Rectify achieves state-of-the-art fidelity under complex degradation. The code is available at https://github.com/Dmsw/SRD-Rectify.

title: RAFTNet: Rationale Adaptive Fusion Target-guided Agent Network for Harmful Meme Detection
abstract: RAFTNet: Rationale Adaptive Fusion Target-guided Agent Network for Harmful Meme Detection.

title: PEER-VAD: Prior-enhanced Event Refinement for Video Anomaly Detection
abstract: Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLM) enable training-free Video Anomaly Detection (VAD). However, most existing methods operate only on isolated frames or short clips. This leads to fragmented predictions due to subtle anomalies and short-term occlusion. We propose Prior-enhanced Event Refinement for Video Anomaly Detection (PEER-VAD). It is a training-free, plug-and-play refinement framework that corrects arbitrary baseline predictions via prior disambiguation and bidirectional window analysis. PEER-VAD transforms fragmented frame-level predictions into semantically consistent event-level predictions. Extensive experiments demonstrate AUC gains, including 4.5% from refining LAVAD on UCF-Crime and 3.1% from refining AnomalyRuler on ShT. Code is available at https://github.com/HaochengY/PEER-VAD.

title: SemStream: Semantic Boundary-Aware Memory for Streaming Video Understanding
abstract: Processing continuous video streams requires multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to maintain temporally coherent memory. Existing architectures predominantly rely on heuristic feature similarity, such as cosine similarity, for memory updates, making them blind to high-level semantics and susceptible to catastrophic fragmentation from camera ego-motion. To overcome this, we construct SemBound-1K, a multi-dimensional soft-labeled dataset that factorizes video boundaries into visual, action, and subject transitions while explicitly penalizing camera noise. Building upon this foundation, we propose SemStream, an intent-driven streaming architecture realized through semantic boundary-aware memory management. SemStream replaces heuristic matching with a learned Semantic Continuity Controller (SCC) for dynamic event partitioning, and employs a Budgeted Episode Merger (BEM) for long-term memory consolidation under strict token constraints. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SemStream achieves state-of-the-art performance, with accuracies of 78.6% on StreamingBench, 74.1% on MLVU, and 62.3% on ODV-Bench. By natively modeling semantic transitions, SemStream effectively prevents memory fragmentation, enabling robust long-horizon reasoning in complex, unconstrained real-world environments. The project page is available at https://jasontan2002.github.io/SemStream.github.io/.

title: Embodied Multimedia: From Multimedia Content to Situated Human-AI Interaction
abstract: Multimedia research, which has traditionally been concerned with the analysis and generation of multimedia content, has increasingly addressed multimodal human behavior. This development is exemplified by current ACM Multimedia Challenges, including POLY-SIM [3], which addresses robust speaker identification under missing-modality and cross-lingual scenarios, MultiMediate [2], which targets engagement estimation across domain, age, and culture, and REACT [4], which focuses on generating appropriate facial reactions in dyadic interactions. Together, these challenges reflect a broader shift from analyzing multimedia content toward analyzing, understanding and generating multimodal behavior in increasingly complex social contexts. The next frontier is to develop embodied AI systems that understand, support, and fluently participate in situated human interaction. We pursue this vision through virtual agents and social robots that facilitate communication between people and AI and increasingly between people themselves. The talk will demonstrate how pretrained multimodal foundation models can be leveraged to create context-aware embodied AI. Drawing on applications in assistive communication, AI-mediated group discussions, and social coaching, the talk will illustrate how embodied agents enabled by these models can help overcome communication barriers, facilitate social interaction, and foster authentic self-expression. At the same time, significant challenges remain in grounding multimodal models in physical and social context, ensuring responsive and coordinated behavior, and evaluating whether apparently socially intelligent behavior is appropriate, robust, and trustworthy [1].

title: Multimodal-Guided Diffusion Model for Composite Image Lighting Adaptation via Curriculum Lighting Learning
abstract: Composite image lighting adaptation aims to adjust the lighting of a composited foreground so that it harmonizes with the illumination of a target background. Recent diffusion models have significantly advanced this task by training on large-scale relighting pairs. However, existing methods often struggle to maintain both content consistency and lighting consistency in composite images. Moreover, the construction of relighting datasets and the corresponding training paradigm for lighting adaptation remain underexplored. To address these challenges, we propose HarmoLight, a multimodal-guided diffusion model for composite image lighting adaptation. Specifically, our model is guided by decoupled content and lighting prompts through a decoupled cross-attention mechanism, enabling more effective control over foreground appearance and illumination adaptation. To effectively derive appropriate lighting guidance, we further introduce a lighting representation distillation strategy that transfers lighting encoding knowledge from a large pre-trained model. In addition, to better facilitate the learning of diverse lighting transformations, we employ a curriculum lighting learning strategy over our specially designed datasets, where training samples are organized according to their lighting adaptation difficulty. Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments on both synthetic datasets and real-world images demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches.

title: Rationale: Rationally Conditional Image Synthesis with Structural Consistency and Distribution Shift
abstract: A paramount challenge in controllable diffusion models is the inherent conflict between guidance signals, such as structure and style, which compete within the latent feature space and lead to visual artifacts. Existing methods attempt to mitigate these conflicts through architectural modifications or heuristic fusion, but often ignore their root cause: the lack of a shared contextual basis among guidance signals. Without a unified structural prior, content and style remain entangled in the feature space, leading to unstable attention dynamics. This paper introduces Rationale, a novel hybrid framework that resolves this conflict by rationally combining a lightweight, trainable style encoder with two parameter-free, inference-time attention guidance modules. Our approach first leverages a dedicated projection network, Resampler, trained on our newly curated, style-balanced Subject-Materials-Style-Set dataset, to encode a reference image into a rich style representation. Then, during generation, our two modules ensure its harmonious application: 1) Relative Self-Attention Guidance actively corrects for structural distortions by steering self-attention queries towards a stable, pre-computed structural prior. 2) Style-Aligned Sparse Attention achieves precise, localized stylization by decoupling content and style at the query-level in the cross-attention mechanism. This hybrid design combines the rich expressive power of a trained encoder with the fine-grained control of dedicated, training-free guidance, avoiding the high costs of test-time optimization. Rationale demonstrates superior performance in structure-preserving stylization and photorealistic material transfer, validated by extensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations, achieving a state-of-the-art LPIPS score of 0.483 and highly preferred stylization quality by human evaluators.

title: Towards Visual-object Triggered Video Event Extraction and Localization for Embodied Security-critical Scenarios
abstract: Traditional event extraction mainly relies on language predicates (e.g., hit and steal ) to characterize events, yet this text-centered paradigm does not fully capture the embodied physical world, where events, especially in embodied security-critical scenarios, are primarily triggered by visual objects rather than language cues. With this in mind, we propose a new Visual-object Triggered Video Event Extraction and Localization (VTrig-E2L) task for Embodied Security-critical Scenarios, aiming to extract and localize structured event tuples (i.e., [trigger-subject and its box, event type, trigger-object and its box]), where trigger-subject and trigger-object refer to the subject and object at the initial event-triggering moment, facilitating early warning. Furthermore, this paper reveals two key challenges in the proposed task: 1) how to effectively incentivize the unified reasoning of explicit language thinking and implicit visual thinking; and 2) how to highlight implicit visual thinking beyond language priors. To tackle these challenges, this paper proposes a new EagleEye approach, i.e., EagleEye acts like an eagle, using implicit visual thinking to scan the scene, spot triggers, and localize events. Specifically, EagleEye incorporates two key components: the Unified Language-Visual Thinking Module (U-LVT) and Causal-guided GRPO Module for Implicit Visual Thinking Enhancement (C-GRPO), to address the above two challenges, respectively. Extensive evaluations on our constructed CoTEvent benchmark show the advantages of EagleEye over several advanced Video-LLMs for the VTrig-E2L task. These results justify the importance of language-visual thinking, especially implicit visual thinking, in VTrig-E2L and demonstrate the effectiveness of EagleEye in highlighting it.

title: UMSBench-v1: A Real-Synthetic Composited Multimodal Benchmark Dataset for Underground Mine Safety
abstract: To fill the gap on benchmark datasets for vision language models (VLM) research on underground mining safety analysis, we introduce UMSBench-v1.0. As the first multimodal VQA benchmark dataset and also the first real-synthetic image dataset on mining safety, it consists of 10,000 real-synthetic underground images and 40,000 question-answer pairs correspondingly, and covers safety reasoning, captioning, understanding and perception over 30 underground mining site types. The synthetic data are generated with newly proposed Image-to-Text-to-Image(I2T2I)mechanism based on refined LLM-driven captioning capabilities, prompting engineering and visual content generation models. Moreover, benchmarking tasks are reformulized as Multiple-Choice Questions(MCQs) with advanced VLMs and human experts as references to archive higher flexibility, scalability and efficiency. State-of-the-art vision language models are benchmarked and finetuned to demonstrate the dataset's effectiveness and potential application. The dataset will be released at https://github.com/BCU-AILAB/UMSBench.

title: A Large-Scale Multi-Modal Benchmark and Robust Text-Free Inference for Breast Ultrasound Video Segmentation
abstract: Breast cancer is one of the leading causes of death among women worldwide, and accurate segmentation of breast ultrasound images is of crucial importance. Compared with static images, videos have advantages in capturing lesions' dynamic and spatial information. However, research on breast tumor ultrasound video segmentation remains extremely limited due to the lack of high-quality publicly available datasets and the high cost of frame-by-frame annotation. In this situation, sparse-frame annotation of videos serves as a more affordable strategy, and diagnostic reports can be used to provide global semantic guidance for videos. However, diagnostic reports are unavailable in advance during clinical diagnosis, which limits the reasoning ability of current multi-modal models. To solve these issues, we construct the first large-scale multi-modal benchmark dataset, containing 1,085 videos with the corresponding clinical diagnostic text and tumor grading information. This dataset establishes a foundation for algorithm research and performance evaluation. Furthermore, we propose a multi-modal training framework with Text-Free inference for Breast tumor ultrasound Video Segmentation (TF-BVS). TF-BVS incorporates a Label-aware Visual-To-Text Optimal Transport module (LV2TOT) to generate pseudo-text token embeddings highly consistent with clinical text distributions, thus enabling inference under text-free conditions in line with clinical workflows. TF-BVS employs a dual-branch joint training strategy, achieving robust segmentation performance even with less annotated training data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TF-BVS achieves state-of-the-art segmentation results on both the proposed multi-modal breast ultrasound dataset and the public VTUS thyroid ultrasound dataset.

title: Learning Explainable Video Saliency Prediction from Reasoning-Annotated Eye-Tracking Supervision
abstract: Understanding visual attention is fundamental to video analysis, as it reveals where viewers focus and provides cues for interpreting dynamic scenes. However, existing eye-tracking benchmarks primarily provide saliency maps as supervision, lacking explicit signals that explain why attention is drawn to specific regions. This limitation hinders the development of explainable video saliency models. To address this gap, we present SGI-ADV (Subjective Gazing Indicators for Attention-Diverse Videos), a large-scale benchmark for learning video attention from reasoning-annotated eye-tracking supervision. SGI-ADV contains eye-tracking data collected from 4,600 participants, along with multi-frame gaze annotations paired with textual explanations that associate attention patterns with salient visual content and temporal dynamics. Building upon this dataset, we propose SalDAR (Saliency Decoding with Attribution and Reasoning), a novel framework that integrates a reason-guided visual decoder into multimodal large language models (MLLMs). SalDAR jointly predicts pixel-level saliency maps and generates human-understandable rationales from multi-frame video inputs, enabling unified modeling of where attention occurs and how it can be explained. Extensive experiments on SGI-ADV demonstrate that SalDAR consistently outperforms existing video saliency methods. Furthermore, evaluations on two widely used public benchmarks, DHF1K and MVS, verify its strong generalization capability. Codes and dataset are available at https://github.com/daisysunset/SalDAR.

title: DIFPA: Boosting Adversarial Transferability via Diffusion-based Importance-aware Feature Pyramid Attack
abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) are known to be vulnerable to adversarial examples, raising serious security concerns in real-world applications. In black-box settings, transfer-based attacks exploit the transferability of adversarial examples crafted on a surrogate model to fool unknown target models, making transferability a central issue in practical adversarial attacks. Recent feature-level transfer attacks improve transferability by perturbing intermediate representations that are more likely to be shared across architectures. However, their effectiveness is still limited by unreliable feature-importance estimation and an over-reliance on single-layer features, which together hinder the accurate localization and suppression of transferable intrinsic features. In particular, existing methods often estimate feature importance from a single input or heuristic transformations, making the resulting indicators easily contaminated by unstable non-robust responses. We observe that, as the diffusion forward process progressively perturbs an input, unstable non-robust responses are gradually attenuated, while semantically relevant robust responses become more concentrated. Inspired by this observation, we propose the Diffusion-based Importance-aware Feature Pyramid Attack (DIFPA), a novel feature-level attack that improves transferability from both importance estimation and hierarchical feature modeling. Specifically, we introduce a Diffusion-Guided Importance Estimator (DGIE), which exploits the diffusion forward marginal as a principled and controllable neighborhood sampler to probe local feature stability, suppress unstable non-robust responses, and produce more reliable feature-importance indicators. We further propose a Hierarchical Feature Pyramid Attack (HFPA), which systematically aggregates important features across multiple layers and exploits the hierarchical semantic diversity of DNNs to suppress transferable intrinsic features in a pyramid manner rather than at a single layer. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DIFPA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving average improvements of 8.17% against normally trained models and 7.92% against defended models.

title: MACE: Multi-Atlas Collaborative Editing for Zero-Shot 3D Scenes
abstract: Text-driven 3D scene editing faces a bottleneck: optimization-based methods often require modifications within diffusion architectures, precluding the use of powerful black-box Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), whereas atlas-based methods support arbitrary MLLMs but suffer from geometric distortion and optical flow failures in wide-baseline scenes. To address these limitations, we propose Multi-Atlas Collaborative Editing (MACE), a novel framework for zero-shot 3D Gaussian Splatting manipulation. MACE adaptively partitions the viewing sphere via local geometric entropy to construct localized, low-distortion neural atlases. These decoupled atlases are then assembled into a unified mosaic, empowering off-the-shelf MLLMs to perform context-aware, globally coherent modifications. To ensure robust 3D reconstruction and multi-view consistency, we introduce a FastVGGT-driven geometry-guided consistency loss that replaces fragile flow heuristics, alongside a direction-aware selection mechanism for final 3DGS fine-tuning. Evaluations indicate that MACE effectively mitigates topological distortion, achieving robust multi-view consistency and semantic alignment with significantly reduced per-prompt editing latency.
